8 Pints AI

8.1 Introduction of the company

Pints.ai is a homegrown Singaporean AI company that builds Generative AI solutions to solve problems faced by the financial sector when it comes to privacy concerns in using public models with their private data.

To achieve this, Pints.ai specializes in an alternative compact language model architecture that can achieve near-ChatGPT performance but yet be able to run on lean hardware like a workstation, laptop, or mobile phone.

Moreover, there are important reasons to invest resources to make LLMs run more efficiently. One, being to save the environment and reduce carbon emissions. And two, to counteract the immensely skewed control of AI by technology behemoths, in the likes of OpenAI and Google.

Our research vision is to uncover the AI architecture that is able to encapsulate the capabilities of leading models such as ChatGPT into a mere downloadable mobile app, very much like how smart algorithm and hardware design made our mobile phone more powerful than a mid-80s supercomputer.

8.2 Key problems that Pints.ai solves

In financial services, analysts are flooded with information and data, a lot of which are confidential and cannot leverage cloud productivity tools or public AI. An on-premise Generative AI solution that Pints provides solves the problem, akin to adding a top-tier analyst that can sift through data and derive insights over a very large dataset efficiently. This helps the financial sector improve productivity immensely, thereby driving up profitability.

8.3 The product

8.3.1 Pint's generative AI productivity suite

To put it across simply, Pint's Generative AI Productivity Suite is essentially akin to having a ChatGPT-equivalent productivity tool deployed on-premise for financial sector services to interact with their internal data through an AI-powered platform.

In addition to that, it can connect to data sources such as networked drives, databases, cloud storages, or mailboxes, so that a user may use natural language to interact with the data, in a similar way to how internet users shift away from Google search to ChatGPT to extract answers in a conversational manner.

In a deeper dive, the solution comprises four main modules under the hood:

The first module is the Pints.ai LLM that has been significantly reduced in size. In the case of a very large model like ChatGPT or Bard, the LLM module alone can handle almost all kinds of queries. The Pints.ai LLM module, however, with a much smaller size, has to depend on the rest of the architecture to culminate in functionality akin to ChatGPT.

The second module is the database module, comprising conventional stores and specialized vector stores, forming the extension of the LLM's memory.

The third module is the retrieval module, which is made up of several NLP models, purposed for helping the LLM recall information more accurately.

Last but not least, the prompt module sits on top of the stack, within which several LLMs decide where to route a request to and what to prompt the LLM with.

8.3.2 Bespoke LLM solution

The Pints Generative AI stack can be modified for other use cases besides information retrieval. At the heart of it, it is simply an AI that is able to understand the user intent and use the available knowledge to fulfill a user-defined objective.

8.4 Application in financial sectors

8.4.1 Insurance companies

8.4.1.1 Use case 1—AI sales co-pilot in insurance

Insurance agents face significant challenges in retaining detailed knowledge of various insurance plans, impacting their ability to provide precise and timely client consultations. Pints.ai introduces an AI-driven sales co-pilot, functioning as a sophisticated knowledge management system. This AI tool offers real-time, interactive support, tailoring responses to specific agent queries, thereby enhancing accuracy in client interactions and decision-making.

8.4.1.2 Use case 2—Streamlining insurance claims with AI automation

Insurance claim processing is traditionally manual and precedent-driven. Pints.ai integrates an AI co-pilot to optimize this process. The AI assists in the preliminary analysis of claims, generating recommendations based on existing precedents. This process not only accelerates claim processing but also ensures consistency and compliance with policy guidelines, thereby improving operational efficiency in claim management.

8.4.1.3 MFOs/wealth management

Wealth managers face similar problems as insurance agents when it comes to recommending an appropriate financial product or fund to their clients. An AI co-pilot can significantly enhance this aspect of wealth management by swiftly searching and identifying funds that align with unique client requests, such as investments in climate-friendly companies or funds with exposure to specific regions like China and South America. The Pints.ai tool empowers wealth managers to provide immediate, informed recommendations, catering to the nuanced investment preferences of their clients.

9 Future prospects

9.1 Emerging trends in AI and blockchain integration

9.1.1 AI and blockchain are two contrasting technologies

The development of AI represents a top-down, centralized control technology model. It relies on the collection and analysis of large amounts of data to improve algorithms and decision models. For example, Google, by collecting user browsing data, can accurately push content and advertisements. The core of this technology lies in centralized data processing and application, emphasizing efficiency and control. However, this centralized approach to data processing has raised concerns about privacy and data security. More and more personal data being used to train AI models not only enhances the efficacy of AI but also exacerbates the risk of privacy breaches. Therefore, ethics in AI, privacy protection, and algorithmic bias have become hot research fields.

Blockchain technology is centered around decentralization and encryption. It provides a bottom-up, decentralized cooperation model. Cryptocurrency is a typical application of this technology, disrupting traditional financial systems and large tech companies’ business models. The decentralized nature of blockchain can, to some extent, protect user privacy and prevent data from being misused by unauthorized centralized institutions. Additionally, blockchain offers a new guarantee for the authenticity of content, which is particularly important in the era of content proliferation created by AI.

When AI integrates with blockchain, the characteristics of both can complement each other but may also create some contradictions. For example, AI's powerful data processing capabilities can be used to optimize the efficiency of blockchain operations, but at the same time, it might threaten the decentralization and anonymity of blockchain. Conversely, blockchain can provide a more secure and transparent data source and usage environment for AI, but this might limit AI's access to and use of large-scale data.

The combination of AI and blockchain is both a technical challenge and a business and ethical opportunity. The interaction of these two technologies will shape the future direction of technological development and have a profound impact on society.

9.2 Potential impact on the global financial landscape

Taking the challenge faced by OpenAI as an example, the essential issue is the difficulty in balancing the relationship between the foundation and the commercial company. The foundation aims to achieve AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) to enhance the overall productivity of human civilization. This process requires financing through a commercial company to solve the problems of computational cost and employee motivation. Essentially, it is a public goods fundraising problem, a challenge that humanity has been unable to solve for thousands of years.

9.3 The significance of open source for public goods

9.3.1 Why do public goods need to be open source?

A core characteristic of public goods is their nonexclusivity and noncompetitiveness. This means that people can share these resources without reducing others’ opportunities to use them. Open-source public goods maximize their value because more people can use and improve them without barriers. For example, open-source software allows users to freely use, study, modify, and distribute software, thereby promoting innovation and rapid development.

9.3.2 The problem of high fees for use

High usage fees indeed restrict the widespread adoption and use of public goods. When only a few can afford it, it loses much of its value as a public good. Moreover, high fees can lead to unfair resource distribution, making resources accessible only to an economic elite.

9.3.3 The limitations of the advertising business model

While advertising can fund public goods, this model has limitations. Advertisers usually target specific audiences, which may not align with the most effective or needed use of public goods. Additionally, reliance on advertising might lead to a decline in the quality of public goods, as they might be designed to attract attention rather than serve the public interest.

9.4 Challenges in public goods fundraising

9.4.1 The importance of incentives

Incentives are key to driving the creation and maintenance of public goods. These incentives can be social, such as recognition, reputation, and satisfaction, or economic, such as direct financial returns. Finding the right incentive mechanisms is crucial for ensuring the quality and sustainability of public goods.

9.4.2 The differing roles and goals of foundations and commercial companies

Foundations usually focus on long-term and public interest goals, like the development of AGI, aiming to enhance the overall productivity of human civilization.

Commercial companies are more concerned with short-term gains, profitability, and sustainability, addressing technical development costs and employee motivation through financing.

9.4.3 The unique challenges of information public goods

Information public goods, like digital content and software, face a unique challenge: the marginal cost of replication is almost zero. This makes it difficult for traditional economic models to adapt, as they are typically based on the production and distribution of physically costly goods. Finding appropriate financing and incentive models for these types of public goods is a major contemporary societal challenge.

9.4.4 AGI as a public good

The development of AGI could bring immense societal benefits, such as improving efficiency, solving complex problems, and fostering technological innovation.

However, as a public good, AGI research might face the “free rider” problem, where individuals or companies are unwilling to invest resources, expecting others’ contributions to yield benefits.

9.4.5 Challenges in fundraising and resource allocation

How can funds be effectively raised to support AGI research while ensuring the rational and efficient use of these funds?

How to balance public and private interests to ensure AGI research is not controlled by a minority of interest groups?

9.5 Solving public goods fundraising problems with blockchain

9.5.1 Data as an asset

In this model, individual data is no longer just a collection of information but is transformed into a valuable asset. This means your personal data, such as shopping preferences, browsing history, or health records, can be seen as valuable resources.

This assetization can be achieved through blockchain technology, ensuring data security, transparency, and immutability. Users have complete control over their data and can choose to sell or license its use.

9.5.2 AI models as protocols

In this system, AI models are no longer the product of a single entity or company but operate based on open, decentralized protocols. These protocols use blockchain to manage and record the use and contributions of data.

AI models are trained based on user-provided data assets, enhancing their intelligence and efficiency. This approach makes the development of AI more democratic and decentralized.

9.5.3 Revenue distribution and use of assets

When AI models are used (for example, for predictive analysis, personalized recommendations, etc.), the generated income is distributed to data contributors according to protocol rules.

This means that if your data is used to train a successful AI model, you will receive a corresponding share of the profits according to the protocol. This mechanism encourages users to share their data while ensuring they receive fair compensation.

Under this framework, fundraising for public goods can be achieved by incentivizing individuals to share their data. Since individual data contributions are directly linked to potential economic benefits, this could motivate more people to participate in supporting public goods or services with their data.

These changes will transform existing business models, including company, investment, and financial services, which will give birth to a new way to build more products that are beneficial to all of humanity.

10 Conclusion

The exploration of AI and blockchain within the financial industry, as detailed in this chapter, reveals a rich narrative of technological advancement, challenges, and vast potential. The integration of case studies like Openfabric, io.net, MathWallet, and Pints AI into this narrative offers a concrete perspective on the real-world implications and applications of these technologies. This comprehensive conclusion synthesizes these elements, reflecting on the journey thus far and envisioning the future landscape shaped by AI and blockchain.

The convergence of AI and blockchain in finance marks a significant evolution in the financial sector. AI's data analysis and predictive modeling capabilities have been instrumental in enhancing areas such as customer service and operational efficiency. MathWallet's implementation of AI in customer service is a prime example, demonstrating the efficiency and scalability AI brings to handling customer queries. This application exemplifies how AI can elevate the customer experience in the financial sector, a critical component for customer retention and satisfaction.

Similarly, blockchain technology, with its inherent transparency and security, has been a cornerstone in reshaping financial transactions, particularly in decentralized finance. Platforms like io.net embody this transformation, showcasing the role of blockchain in creating secure and efficient financial networks. Io.net's contribution to the financial industry highlights how blockchain can facilitate secure, transparent financial exchanges, a foundational aspect of modern finance.

The real-world applications of AI and blockchain in the financial industry are diverse and impactful. Openfabric, for instance, demonstrates the innovative use of AI in creating an ecosystem for developing and deploying AI algorithms on the blockchain. This integration underscores how blockchain can enhance the trustworthiness and traceability of AI applications, addressing key concerns such as data integrity and security. Pints AI, on the other hand, showcases AI's immense potential in data processing and decision support within the financial sector. By efficiently managing large datasets, Pints AI exemplifies AI's role in enhancing productivity and driving profitable decision-making in finance. These cases collectively highlight the diverse applications of AI and blockchain, from customer interaction to data management and transaction security. Io.net exemplifies the use of blockchain in creating secure and efficient financial transaction networks. This platform demonstrates blockchain's capacity to revolutionize financial transactions, providing a secure and transparent environment for financial exchanges. MathWallet leverages AI to provide efficient customer service, supporting multiple languages and handling a large number of queries simultaneously. This application demonstrates AI's role in enhancing customer experience and operational efficiency in the financial sector.

While the potential of AI and blockchain is immense, navigating challenges such as data privacy, regulatory compliance, and the complexities of integrating these technologies is crucial for their successful application in finance. The cases discussed provide insights into how these challenges can be addressed, showcasing both the potential and the hurdles of implementing AI and blockchain in financial systems.

In conclusion, the integration of AI and blockchain in the financial industry represents a paradigm shift in technological innovation. As the financial industry continues to evolve, the roles of AI and blockchain are becoming increasingly central, promising new opportunities for innovation, efficiency, and inclusivity. The journey of integrating these technologies into finance is ongoing, with their full impact yet to be fully realized. As AI and blockchain continue to mature and their applications become more widespread, they are set to further transform the financial industry, ushering in new growth opportunities and reshaping economic models.

Chapter 13 Transformation of digital banking back-office operations using AI

  1. Alan Megargel
  2. Venky Shankararaman
  3. Obuchettiar Krishnaraj Arul
  4. School of Computing and Information Systems, Singapore Management University, Singapore, Singapore

Abstract

Over the years, banks have been strategically using digital technologies to help transform various aspects of their business. More recently, this strategy has evolved into one of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven digital augmentation of the bank's processes, products, and channels. In fact, AI is playing a pivotal role in driving digital transformation across the entire spectrum of banking operations, encompassing the front, middle, and back office. In the front office, AI-powered chatbots are enhancing customer interactions, providing personalized recommendations, and streamlining routine inquiries. In the middle office, AI is helping to optimize risk management and compliance, portfolio management, and performing risk analytics related to the portfolios. In the back office, there has been experimentation on using AI, for example, streamlining Know-Your-Customer (KYC) procedures, automating data entry and reconciliation, and automating other tedious tasks. However, AI solutions in the back office still lag the front and middle offices. In the back office, banks have been more focused on process automation rather than automating and enhancing the decision-making within the process. In this chapter, a case-study-centered methodology is employed to delineate the diverse realms where AI can be used to enhance the back-office operations of a bank, spanning across retail, corporate, and investment banking. It then describes the underlying data pipeline that will be needed for aiding AI-enabled decision-making, along with the management implications and a maturity model for guiding the AI adoption in bank back-office operations.

Keywords

Digital bank

Front office

Middle office

Back office

Automation

Artificial intelligence

Machine learning

1 Introduction

There are traditional banks that claim to be digital because they offer online channels (e.g., internet/mobile banking). However, a true digital bank must also have digitalized its internal banking operations (e.g., account origination, fulfillment, settlement), such that these core business processes are fully automated without human interaction. As a rule, even business exception handling (e.g., handling a nonperforming loan) should be fully automated. A fully automated digital bank will operate at a much lower cost than a traditional bank, and the cost savings can be forwarded to customers in terms of better rates and higher yields.

Besides offering better rates and higher yields to customers, a digital bank should be able to deliver personalized cross-sell offers (e.g., low-interest loans, merchant discounts) to customers in real time at the precise moment in time when the bank has the customer's attention, at the point of sale, or at any time the customer is interacting with the bank for any reason [1]. Real-time inbound marketing has been found to be much more effective in generating revenue as compared to traditional outbound direct marketing [2]. Customers who have opted in for personalized real-time offers will be impressed that the bank has an accurate understanding of their financial needs, and this capability will help the bank to establish a good reputation, especially with the younger generations (“digital natives”) who have become accustomed to similar capabilities offered by technology giants and eCommerce companies.

In this chapter, we first describe a model digital bank from a customer perspective, in three tiers: retail/SME, wholesale, and investment digital bank. Second, we cover previous work related to our topic. Third, we present four case studies of banks that are currently transforming/digitalizing their back-office operations, including two traditional commercial banks, a traditional investment bank, and a new online-only digital bank. Then we identify the back-office operations that can be automated using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and/or Machine Learning (ML), supported by a common data pipeline. Finally, we discuss the management implications of AI/ML automation.

2 Model digital bank

Digital banks should have no physical branches. Customer onboarding should be fully automated and should allow customers to open bank accounts without any interaction with bank staff. Online channels should have chatbots to guide customers through any process or to answer any questions, with an option to chat with a human if needed. A digital bank should have call center support to handle customer cases (e.g., transaction disputes). Table 1 lists the features of a model digital bank from a customer's perspective.

Table 1

Features of a model digital bank.
Feature Description
No physical branches Fully online. No face-to-face interaction with bank staff is required for any reason.
Automated customer onboarding Face and ID video scan. Link to national ID registry. Document uploads for corporates: company incorporation, shareholder agreement, and annual financial reports.
Self-service banking transactions Fully online opening/closing deposit accounts, applying for loans, performing fund transfers and bill payments, setting up standing instructions, trade booking, and settlement.
Personalized real-time offers Next-Best-Offers (NBOs), personalized for each customer and generated from historical and ongoing financial needs analysis, are queued up for delivery at the customer's next interaction with the bank, e.g., any financial transaction.
Chatbots Chatbots guide customers through any process, with an option to chat with a human if needed, and have access to the customer's profile to provide advice within the context and specific financial needs of the customer.
Call center support Call center support to handle urgent customer cases (e.g., transaction disputes). Call center operators have a total view of all accounts and credit facilities the customer may have so that they are equipped to resolve any problem.

2.1 Three tiers of digital banks

We can define three tiers of digital banks: one to cover the retail and SME customer segments, one to cover the wholesale banking needs of large corporations engaged in international trade, and one to cover the investment needs of high-net-worth private banking customers and other institutional investors. Each of these three tiers provides the features of a model digital bank listed in Table 1.

2.1.1 Retail/SME digital bank

Retail/SME customers have full self-service capability to open deposit accounts, transfer funds, make payments, set up standing instructions, and apply for simple credit products, with little or no interaction with bank staff. Retail loan products include home mortgages, vehicle loans, education loans, and personal loans. There is a rich online user experience with an emphasis on simplicity and superior service delivery, including personalized cross-sell offers and financial advice.

SME credit products include fixed asset loans, working capital finance, invoice finance, and purchase order finance. The SME offering includes all the banking services aimed at making business more productive and profitable, including cash management facilities: cash concentration, interest optimization, payroll services, and collections.

2.1.2 Corporate (wholesale) digital bank

Corporate customers have full self-service capability to open deposit accounts in multiple different currencies, transfer funds domestically and internationally, and apply for wholesale credit facilities with little or no interaction with bank staff. The wholesale offering includes all the banking products needed to support international trade, including letters of credit, banker guarantees, trust receipts, and export factoring. To support foreign currency payments associated with international trade, a full set of treasury products is offered, including FX trading, FX risk management (FX hedging), liquidity management, and FX forward contracts. There should be a rich online user experience for corporate finance officers with an emphasis on simplicity, parameterization and control, full visibility of accounts, and profit optimization, including targeted situational financial advice.

2.1.3 Investment digital bank

Institutional investors and high-net-worth private banking clients have self-service capability to start and complete the full client onboarding process including automated KYC identification, Customer Due Diligence (CDD), Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD), identification of investment portfolio needs and constraints and risk appetite, and the uploading of required documents, e.g., company incorporation, board resolution. The automated process involves identifying a wider multinational network of family and business relationships and company structures and entities that need to be considered holistically to build a full understanding of the client profile. With comprehensive client profiles, automated prospecting and product recommendations are provided to client advisors with prequalified leads, actionable insights, and talking points.

3 Related work

In this section, we will cover related work in the use of AI in digital banking.

3.1 Use of AI in digital banking

In recent years, with the advent of AI technologies, digital banking innovations have been undergoing a paradigm shift with a focus on going beyond simplistic process automation to intelligent processes that require both AI and humans to collaborate [3]. The innovations have impacted the front, middle, and back offices of traditional banks and, in many cases, thus blurred the lines between the distinct functional roles of these divisions. According to McKinsey, the use of AI and analytics can potentially unlock US$1TN of value for banks [4]. Besides these benefits, traditional banks are under constant threat from digital disruptors in the form of fintech that leverages AI and other innovative technologies to offer enhanced, flexible services at lower costs [5].

3.1.1 Front office

For front-office operations, AI has been used to enhance customer experience, streamline processes, and improve overall operational efficiency [6]. As the use of direct service interaction with customers is labor-intensive, banks have been using AI to automate this process and enhance customer agent productivity. According to McKinsey, virtual assistants and conversational interfaces at the front office form about 32% of the total AI implementations [4]. A very common example is the use of AI-powered chatbots or virtual assistants where the customer interacts with a digital bot to help answer queries and solve problems before any human staff gets involved [7]. Bhattacharya and Sinha's survey of Indian banks identifies a number of use cases for chatbot assistance provided to customers, which include answering questions related to account balance and statements, accelerating loan decisions, supporting the customer's financial and securities transactions, bill payments, and providing reminders on credit card and transaction patterns [8]. Chatbots can access a wide set of information, both pertaining to one customer and those related to current product offerings and market conditions. Besides answering queries, some chatbots can help in providing personalized recommendations. For example, advice on achieving financial goals by suggesting investment options, suggesting suitable products, and budget allocation based on unique spending habits. There have been several successful implementations of chatbots or virtual assistants [5,9,10]. For example, a virtual assistant developed by BNP Paribas Personal Finance in Spain helped to reduce queries managed by call center agents by 46 percent [11]. An example of widespread adoption is the use of Erica, a virtual assistant developed by Bank of America, which received 135 million requests in 2020 with a user base of over 20 million [12].

With recent developments in AI-driven biometric authentication methods, such as facial recognition and fingerprint scanning, many of the front-office operations for secure customer authentication during in-branch visits or digital transactions have been enabled through AI tools [13]. Another popular trend is the use of robo-advisors that analyze customer financial goals, risk tolerance, and market trends to recommend personalized investment strategies. For example, “Acorns Later” is an investment account added to the Acorns application that recommends a retirement account and portfolio to customers based on their age, income, gender, and other factors [14].

3.1.2 Middle office

The middle office is responsible for various critical activities such as risk management and compliance, portfolio management, and risk analytics related to the portfolios. ML algorithms, particularly those utilizing predictive analytics, assist in examining market trends, identifying investment opportunities, and optimizing portfolio allocations. For example, Jang and Seong have developed an AI-based algorithm that helps to optimize portfolios by combining reinforcement learning with portfolio theory. With continuous learning, the AI algorithm can dynamically change the portfolio according to market trends, thus optimizing annualized returns and maximum drawdown [15].

AI technologies, including robotic process automation (RPA) and natural language processing (NLP), are applied to automate trade confirmation, reconciliation, and settlement processes. AI helps to process huge swathes of data rapidly and accurately and presents succinct analysis to human managers, who can then make data-driven decisions. Earlier, electronic routing algorithms were used to match buy and sell orders from traders to various stockbrokers and to trading systems to fulfill the orders. Usually, nearly 30% of these trades processed on behalf of asset managers require manual intervention to complete, thus leading to delays. Hence, banks have been exploring ML techniques using predictive analytics to help alleviate this problem. For example, Smart Chaser, a tool implemented by BNP Paribas Securities Services, utilizes predictive analysis to automate trade processing by optimizing the trading routes using historical data as well as the opportunity cost for each execution route. In this way, the probability of success is mapped out for each possible execution route. With the tool, it is possible to predict the likelihood of delayed “trade matching,” along with the details that contribute to the delay, thus enabling the middle-office operational team to intervene early [16].

Risk departments managing the risk associated with portfolios usually monitor a large amount of data across many counterparties and transactions. Usually, data sources exist in many mediums across geographies and languages. One approach to handle this complexity is to focus on high-priority lists and then sample the remaining data on a rotation basis. Using NLP and text analytics techniques, it is possible to extract, review, and filter content relevant to a specific risk-monitoring purpose [3]. Additionally, with AI it is now possible to develop advanced risk analytics and stress testing models. AI algorithms can process large datasets in real time, assess risk exposures, and simulate various market scenarios. Another relevant area is in credit risk modeling, whereby AI models can help assess the creditworthiness of borrowers by analyzing diverse sets of data, including financial history, economic indicators, and industry trends.

3.1.3 Back office

Though there has been a lot of interest in using AI in the banking industry, there has been very little transformation in the back office. This is despite nearly 60% of customer dissatisfaction sources originating in the back office [17]. Most digital transformation efforts have been addressing areas such as human resources, legal, or reconciliation. To remove inefficiencies in operations, it is not sufficient to just modernize the infrastructure. For example, Zeghmouli quotes that “we, human beings, need to analyze, define and organise the back offices of 2025” [18]. The back office is responsible for efficient operations that cover functions such as overall risk management, compliance, data processing, and bank's internal processes. Understanding the implications, challenges, and advancements of AI in the back office is essential for comprehensively gauging the overall impact of AI in a bank.

RPA has seen widespread implementation in the back office, where repetitive and rule-based tasks, such as data entry, reconciliation, and transaction processing, are automated by using software robots. For example, at Eurobank, 20 processes within the Loan Administration Division were automated within 6 months using RPA. One such process was distributing received payments for credit card debts to the correct credit card account. Before automation, this process took around 4 h per day for seven employees. The automation of this process saved two FTEs, reduced time for payment processing, and lowered the error rate to 0% [19]. One challenge with developing RPA-based solutions is the time-consuming task of setting the parameters. It works very well for high-volume, simple tasks that are based on predefined rules and workflows and use structured data. Going forward, banks need to integrate RPA with ML algorithms that facilitate self-learning and continuous improvement and can work well with both structured and unstructured data [18].

Another popular application of AI in the back office is the streamlining of customer onboarding processes and KYC procedures. Using NLP and ML, it is easier to extract and analyze information from unstructured data sources such as documents and forms. This helps with the automation of identity verification and document validation, which in turn expedites the onboarding process while ensuring compliance with regulatory requirements. For example, EY reports that by using AI for KYC, the time required was reduced from an average of 18 min to less than 1 min. Additionally, the bank was able to reduce over 6000 manual resources allocated to KYC processing [20].

In 2020, institutions spent an estimated US$214B on financial-crime compliance [21]. With traditional approaches such as rule-based systems, the banks cannot keep up with the innovative approaches adopted by criminals. Banks need to move to AI solutions that leverage ML. ML can be used for Antimoney Laundering (AML) compliance in back-office operations by automating the analysis of large volumes of transactions and detecting patterns that may indicate money laundering or other illicit activities. This enhances the efficiency and accuracy of AML processes [21]. For example, a Singapore bank, UOB, has implemented a ML-based solution that enables it to pinpoint higher-priority cases from the more than 5700 average monthly suspicious transaction alerts [22]. This helped to focus on these cases and swiftly investigate potential money laundering attempts. Han et al. have developed a framework that utilizes advanced NLP and deep learning techniques to facilitate next-generation AML technologies [23].

The finance industry is subject to an ever-evolving regulatory landscape. To efficiently handle and implement the regulations within the bank, AI has been employed to streamline compliance processes and facilitate accurate and timely regulatory reporting. Automated systems utilizing NLP and ML algorithms can interpret complex regulatory requirements and ensure banks adhere to compliance standards. Studies highlight the efficiency gains and reduced compliance risks associated with AI implementation in the back office. Urazova proposes three areas where AI technologies can be used for managing regulatory requirements [24]. First, the integration of ML with traditional regulatory technology (RegTech) focused on improving the efficiency of meeting the requirements of central banks and other regulators of financial markets. Second, helping banks to organize their internal activities such as preparing internal reports, forecasting cash flows, and staff performance assessments. Third, using AI in activities related to servicing private and corporate clients, such as background analysis, checking the correctness of paperwork, and assessment of the creditworthiness of borrowers.

Like any business, the back office in a bank is a critical area for safeguarding sensitive information. AI is increasingly utilized to fortify cybersecurity measures, detect anomalies, and prevent fraudulent activities. ML algorithms can analyze patterns, identify irregularities, and raise alerts in real time, thereby strengthening the security posture of banks. Kaur et al. provide a systematic literature review on the use of AI for the provision of cybersecurity in any organization across five different cybersecurity functions, namely, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover [25].

3.2 Summary of related work

In summary, as seen from the literature review, back-office implementation of AI solutions in banks is lagging as compared to front and middle-office implementations. Banks must understand that the potential uses of AI in the back office go beyond process automation and that AI-based decision-making is needed within the process. Most banks have not yet invested in AI solutions for their back offices [18]. The published literature reviewed here covers the potential use of AI in a broader context across multiple geographical locations. To better understand the evolving landscape of the use of AI in driving digital transformation of the back office, the next section will focus on four case studies from the SE Asia region.

4 Case studies

This section summarizes four case studies of banks that are currently transforming/digitalizing their back-office operations using AI, including two traditional commercial banks, a traditional investment bank, and a new online-only digital bank. This multiple case study was interview-based, where each bank's interview included one or more participants. The interviews were audio recorded, and the transcripts were anonymized.

4.1 Case study 1

Bank-A

Profile

Bank-A is a large commercial bank headquartered in SE Asia, supporting retail/SME and corporate customers. The interviewee was the bank's Chief Information Officer. From an operational perspective, they are still very much a traditional bank, with branch offices and manual back-office processes.

Back-office automation

Focus is on workflow automation using business process management (BPM) tools, where 60%–70% of manual processes are now managed via BPM. The BPM tool provides a transaction-centric view of the data. Retail loan fulfillment, e.g., disbursement of funds, is managed under BPM. Corporate loans, e.g., working capital and invoice financing, are “bespoke” products and are not managed via BPM. The bank does not consider Straight Through Processing (STP) as part of operations, i.e., they only consider manual processes as part of operations. STP processing is done via vendor applications such as Murex for FX/remittance.

Technology/AI adoption

In the advanced experimentation stage, using AI to comprehend and make decisions on trade documents, e.g., letters of credit (LC), invoices, guarantees, etc., using NLP models. Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) models are used for credit evaluation and approvals. Experimenting with generative AI to support call centers. Experimenting with replacing the human “maker” with AI for “maker-checker” processes. Exploring opportunities to automate trade finance using AI, e.g., verifying export documents meet conditions of the matching LC and checking invoices for trade-related fraud and money laundering patterns.

Management of data pipeline/tech stack

For data analytics outside of operations, consolidation to a single data lake has enabled them to ingest data at scale, define a metadata model, and create a common data pipeline. A rules-based access matrix democratizes data access and enables data scientists to import data and develop their own reusable models.

Benefits of AI

Five-year CAGR shows an increase in revenue by 41% and an increase in volume by 10% while maintaining the same number of back-office operations staff. Productivity gains have been invested in new product initiatives.

4.2 Case study 2

Bank-B

Profile

Bank-B is a large commercial bank headquartered in SE Asia, supporting retail/SME and corporate customers. The interviewee was the bank's Chief Data Officer. From an operational perspective, they are still very much a traditional bank, with branch offices and manual back-office processes.

Back-office automation

The bank has traditionally used classic BPM and document-centric workflow engines to automate its back-office operations (e.g., loan ops and trade ops) and RPA to automate its front-office repetitive tasks. Regarding AI, the bank has prioritized AI model development for its middle-office functions (e.g., compliance and risk) over the past 10 years and has now shifted its focus to AI-enabling its back-office operations.

Technology/AI adoption

AI-enablement of the back office started with common functions that all operations need including information extraction from documents, customer onboarding, KYC, AML, and fraud detection and prevention. Examples given include extracting information from treasury term sheets and extracting compliance instructions from Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) payment messages. For corporate banking, they use AI for intraday and end-of-day cash flow forecasting and scenario testing on how interest rate changes may affect the customer's balance sheet. Around 70% of the bank's compliance alerts from adverse name screening are closed by AI, freeing up about 20 people. For personalized real-time inbound marketing, the bank deploys 250 million AI-generated offers per year. For nonperforming loans, AI is used to predict which customers are likely to default along with the most effective channel for handling collections activities. For infrastructure support, AI is used to monitor about 300 system logs in real time and alert data center staff on performance issues. Internally, the bank has an AI chatbot for operations staff to ask questions about internal policies and procedures and help developers auto-generate code.

Management of data pipeline/tech stack

The bank maintains a classic on-premises Enterprise Data Warehouse (EDW) for regulatory reporting but has transitioned all other data used for analytics to a private cloud environment that serves as its common data lake, supporting the whole bank. They have about 20 source systems that feed real-time data into their data lake to support real-time marketing offers, real-time fraud detection, real-time hedging, etc. The bank has a center of excellence for advanced analytics, including 70 data scientists, 30 data engineers, 40 traditional analysts, and 150 analytics “translators” who work with the front-office business teams.

Benefits of AI

The bank has deployed about 250 AI models to save time and money, reduce risk, and help customers make better investment decisions. Around 4 million decisions per day are AI-enabled, and this number is projected to increase to 10 million per day by 2025. Over the past 10 years, the bank has reduced its back-office operations staff by 5% per year, while the bank's transaction volumes have doubled over that same period. The productivity of bank staff has improved by 50%.

4.3 Case study 3

Bank-C

Profile

Bank-C is a large investment bank headquartered in Europe, supporting institutional and wealth management (private banking) clients. The interviewee was from the wealth management side of the bank. They are around 10 years into an initiative to transform from a traditional to a digital wealth management bank.

Back-office automation

The bank's back-office operations center mainly supports its front-office (client-facing) Client Advisors (CAs) on client onboarding and lead generation. Traditionally, client onboarding had been a very manual process, taking 4–6 weeks, but now AI-based evaluations are performed in real time including risk profiling. Continuous KYC screening is performed automatically, including daily checks for material changes in client circumstances and negative news, which may trigger alerts. Traditionally, CAs did not have enough actionable insights from the market and preferred their own warm leads via networking instead of the ones assigned to them, but now an AI-based engine automatically generates prequalified leads along with portfolio recommendations and talking points. Transaction fulfillment is automated from trade booking through settlement. Transactions are monitored for fraud.

Technology/AI adoption

For continuous KYC, news articles are scanned, Named Entity Recognition (NER) models are used to link different names of people and entities, and these links are then matched to client profiles using Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and transformer-based models. Hierarchical sentiment analysis is used to quantify relevant negative sentiment associated with the client. For lead generation, knowledge graphs are used to reveal relationships between existing and prospective clients, and Graph Neural Network (GNN) models with constraints (e.g., size of funds, industry) are used to make predictions. For talking points, NLP models are used to curate relevant, persuasive information snippets justifying the proposed investment. For portfolio recommendations, Reinforcement Learning (RL) models are created for each category of client based on their investment portfolio and risk appetite. For Sustainable Investing (SI), customized BERT models are used to scan Environment, Society, and Governance (ESG) reports of companies.

Management of data pipeline/tech stack

Real-time data streaming of market data is mission-critical. The bank is developing a data mesh architecture to enable federated data ownership, such that each department manages its own data. They are transitioning to private cloud storage, which has increased their focus on cybersecurity, including packet-level monitoring and analysis. No third-party APIs are allowed.

Benefits of AI

Over the past 10 years, 30% of manual processes have been automated using AI. With efficiency gains, back-office staff have been redeployed to other departments. CA's can now support twice as many clients, with improved quality of advice.

4.4 Case study 4

Bank-D

Profile

Bank-D is a licensed digital bank headquartered in SE Asia, operating under a regulator-issued digital banking license, supporting retail/SME and corporate customers. The interviewee was the bank's Chief Risk Officer. The bank has no physical branches or ATM machines.

Back-office automation

Loan operations (unsecured loans) are AI-enabled and fully automated, including loan origination, credit approval, loan disbursement, and collections. Unsecured loans are approved within 1 min, as creditworthiness is based on the customer's past payment performance within the bank's group ecosystem including a ride-share provider and a telco. ML-based credit scorecards are continually improved using champion-challenger models, such that subsequent credit drawdowns are priced based on the customer's past repayment performance. AI models are used to predict credit losses due to nonperforming loans and prioritize collections activities according to different levels of delinquency.

Technology/AI adoption

The bank's infrastructure is fully cloud-based including a multi-tenant Software-As-A-Service (SaaS) Core Banking System (CBS), rather than a dedicated CBS typically deployed on-premises by traditional banks. They have a small team of 30 data scientists to develop AI models.

Management of data pipeline/tech stack

The bank's data pipeline and data lake are cloud-based and support AI models for the entire bank. Their data lake is comprised of more than 250 fields sourced from across the bank's group ecosystem, i.e., the bank, the ride-share provider, and the telco. The data pipeline features and AI models are continuously refined, using daily reports that correlate model performance against a benchmark.

Benefits of AI

The bank has been AI-enabled from the beginning since they started taking deposits less than 2 years ago. With AI in place, the bank's back-office operations are already more than 97% automated. Front-office customer service, with AI chatbots in place, is expected to scale to 5× business volumes over the next few years with minimal additional headcount. Surveys show that their customer satisfaction exceeds 80%.

Table 2 provides a comparison of the four banks studied earlier as to their automation of back-office operations using AI.

Summary of case studies.
Bank Bank type Back-office adoption of AI
Bank-A Traditional Commercial Bank The bank is highly regarded as a digital bank due to its online customer-facing digital channels. However, beyond NPL for digesting documents, AI is still in the experimental stage as applied to back-office automation. Mostly, they employ rules-based decision-making under BPM.
Bank-B Traditional Commercial Bank The bank has an effective AI center of excellence in place to support bank-wide AI development. The bank's AI is at an advanced stage for middle office support of compliance and risk processes, as well as its back-office support of treasury, trade, payments, loan collections, real-time cross-selling, and fraud detection and prevention.
Bank-C Traditional Investment Bank While the front-office CA support of clients is relationship-based, as is the nature of wealth management banking, this bank has successfully transformed its back office from manual to mostly AI-enabled digital operations, resulting in higher benefits realization for clients and higher trade volumes for the bank.

All their infrastructure is cloud-based, at a low cost, and 97% of their back-office operations are fully automated. As a result, their customer satisfaction scores exceed 80%.

5 Back-office operations suitable for automation using AI

Based on our multiple case studies of four representative banks, we have derived a set of back-office operations in each type of bank (retail, corporate, investment) that are suitable for automation using AI, as shown in Fig. 1. Also included are the relevant common back-office operations that are present in all bank types.

The block Back Office Operations is divided into four categories: Retail Banking, Corporation Banking, Investment Banking, and Common Functions. The components under each category are as follows: Retail Banking includes Loan Origination and Fulfilment, Credit Scoring and Approval, Personalized Marketing, and Collections Optimization. Corporation Banking includes Credit Underwriting and Risk Assessment, Cash Management and Forecasting, Trade Finance and Supply Chain Finance, Loan Structuring, Contract Analysis, and Foreign Exchange and Treasury Operations. Investment Banking includes Portfolio Management, Market Research and Analysis, Market Risk Management, Trade Confirmation and Settlement, Trade Surveillance, and Securities Lending and Borrowing. Common Functions include Document Digitization, Customer Onboarding and KYC, Customer Relationship Management, and Fraud Detection and Prevention.

The following sections provide more detail about AI usage in back-office operations for each bank type, including one section on common functions.

5.1 Retail banking operations

Use of AI in retail banking operations.
Operation Use of AI in retail banking operations
Loan Origination and Fulfillment
  • • Replace human data entry by automatically extracting and entering data from loan application forms and associated documentation while ensuring lending practices adhere to relevant financial and legal regulations.
  • • Handle and reply to emails and messages from customers, forwarding more complicated questions to loan officers.
  • • Provide immediate responses to customer inquiries regarding loan status via chatbot.
Credit Scoring and Approval
  • • Ingest and analyze unstructured data such as utility bills and social media posts to evaluate the creditworthiness of customers with limited credit history.
  • • Assess historical financial activity, such as savings and spending patterns, as inputs for credit scoring, as well as dynamically update credit scores based on real-time transactions.
  • • Improve the quality of credit decisions using historical data to predict the probability of loan defaults.
  • • Provide a precise risk profile that can be used to set interest rates and loan terms more accurately than traditional approaches.
Personalized Marketing
  • • Analyze a customer's transaction history and affinities to predict future financial needs, facilitating the delivery of personalized targeted product offerings (e.g., deposits, loans, investments).
  • • Continuously improve targeted offers based on real-time transactions or recent changes in the customer's financial behavior or life-stage events (e.g., changing jobs, retiring).
  • • Adjust the content and tone of marketing messages, as well as the optimal delivery timings, for each individual customer based on past communications.
Collections Optimization
  • • Prioritize collection efforts by identifying accounts that are more likely to go into default.
  • • Personalize repayment plans depending on the customer's financial situation and payment history.
  • • Reach out to customers via chatbot about outstanding debts and assist them with the payment process.
  • • Ensure collection practices adhere to relevant legal regulations via AI-based compliance tools.

Operation Use of AI in corporate banking operations
Credit Underwriting and Risk Assessment
  • • Analyze large unstructured datasets, such as market trends, macroeconomic indicators, and financial statements, to assess the creditworthiness of corporate clients.
  • • Model different risk scenarios based on historical trends and current market conditions, and continuously adjust these risk assessments based on changes in the customer's industry outlook or financial performance.
  • • Optimize the bank's credit portfolio, balancing risk vs return, and perform stress testing simulations to predict the impact of different economic and market conditions on the credit portfolio.
Cash Management and Forecasting
  • • Optimize working capital for their corporate customers by predicting the best timing for paying suppliers and collecting payments.
  • • Optimize liquidity management by predicting and recommending short-term investments during cash surplus conditions and financing during cash deficiency conditions.

Trade Finance and Supply Chain Finance
  • • Ingest and analyze data from trade documents such as letters of credit, bills of lading, and invoices; verify authenticity; and match data between documents to check for accuracy.
  • • Verify trades are compliant with international regulations, can verify countries of origin are not on sanctions lists, and can identify trade patterns that indicate money laundering activity and take automatic action.
  • • Automate the matching of shipping documents and purchase orders. Enable dynamic invoice discounting for early payments, optimizing the cash flow for both buyers and sellers.
Loan Structuring
  • • Analyze the corporate customer's profile to tailor loan structures based on their specific needs, current financial health, historical credit performance, and collateral valuation.
  • • Run simulations to predict the impact of different macroeconomic and market conditions on loan structuring decisions.
  • • Implement risk-based pricing (e.g., interest rates, fees) to balance the corporate customer's specific loan terms against the bank's overall exposure to credit risk.
Contract Analysis
  • • Ingest and analyze contractual terms and clauses related to legal constraints, penalties, and rights to identify financial risks and legal liabilities the bank may potentially be exposed to.
  • • Verify contract compliance against internal policies, regulatory requirements, and relevant laws.
  • • Monitor upcoming contractual events such as reporting deadlines and financial obligations, and alert relevant parties.
Foreign Exchange and Treasury Operations
  • • Analyze a corporate customer's treasury positions, predict adverse FX rate movement in the market based on current market conditions and financial news reports, identify currencies where the customer is overexposed to FX rate movement, and automatically execute hedging trades to avoid losses. The same market analysis and automatic hedging capability can be applied to manage the bank's own internal treasury positions.

6 Common data pipeline

This section compiles the common concerns shared by the four banks in our case study regarding data pipeline management. To support the use of AI across retail, corporate, and investment banking functions, it is important for a bank to architect, develop, and maintain a common data pipeline. A common data pipeline serves as the foundation for AI-enabled applications, ensuring an efficient and reliable aggregation, processing, and analysis of large amounts of data through to the bank's common data lake. Data sources include customer transactions, market data, communications records, and system logs. A common data pipeline enables standardized data governance and compliance processes whereby data handling rules and regulatory policies can be uniformly applied and managed. A common data pipeline, centrally managed by a data center of excellence, fosters a more collaborative environment and breaks down data silos whereby innovations and insights are shared across the bank. Fig. 2 illustrates the components of a common data pipeline.

The process starts with Business Events, which branches into Realtime Data Streaming and Workflow Automation. Realtime Data Streaming further branches into Internal Data Sources and External Data Sources. Both Internal and External Data Sources lead to Data Preprocessing, which then connects to Feature Engineering. Feature Engineering leads to Monitoring and Logging. Workflow Automation connects to API Integration, which leads to Model Deployment. Model Deployment connects to Data Storage (Data Lake) and Model Development. Data Storage (Data Lake) connects to Feature Engineering and Backup & Recovery. Model Development connects to Model Deployment and Feedback Loop. Feedback Loop connects back to Workflow Automation. The entire process is governed by Data Governance.

6.1 Data sources

A bank's data pipeline is fed by a diverse set of internal and external data sources, each supplying various information for aiding in AI-enabled decision-making. Internal data sources include (a) core account-keeping systems that provide customer account balances, real-time and historic financial transactions, and loan repayment histories useful for understanding the customer's financial situation and behavior, and (b) Customer Relationship Management (CRM) systems, call center systems, and digital channels (e.g., mobile apps and websites) that provide insights into customer service experiences and preferences.

External data sources include (a) real-time market data feeds that provide FX rates, stock prices, treasury bills, and other exchange-traded instruments; (b) market news reports that provide insights on industry sectors and individual companies; (c) economic indicators such as Gross Domestic Product (GDP), Consumer Price Index (CPI), inflation rates, and unemployment rates that provide insights into the financial health of markets; (d) credit bureaus that contribute information on customers’ creditworthiness; and (e) social media feeds that provide unstructured data that can be analyzed to understand public sentiment impacting customer behavior.

6.2 Data preprocessing and feature engineering

Data preprocessing and feature engineering steps transform source data into a structure suitable for AI models. At the data preprocessing stage, data extracted from internal and external sources is cleaned, e.g., duplicate records removed, and repaired, e.g., missing values populated with defaults. The data is then segmented to represent different transaction types or customer groups so that AI models can effectively be applied across diverse scenarios. Finally, the data is normalized or scaled uniformly to prevent feature bias.

Data scientists then engineer features such as average account balance, credit card usage patterns, or frequency of overdrafts, derived from the preprocessed structured data to enhance the AI model's accuracy in making predictions. Techniques such as time series analysis are used to better capture underlying patterns in temporal data such as interest rates and stock prices to support investment decisions. Feature engineering requires data scientists to have banking domain knowledge, for example, calculating financial ratios (e.g., debt-to-income, loan-to-value) for loan processing. Finally, the data is split into training datasets, representative samples used to train AI models, ensuring their effectiveness and accuracy.

6.3 Common data lake for AI model development and deployment

There are advantages for a bank to implement a common data lake to support all its AI model development and deployment. The data lake serves as a consolidated repository of data streamed from both internal and external sources. Such centralization of data and its management is important for ensuring a consistent level of data quality and accuracy across a diverse set of AI applications, e.g., risk profiling, product recommendations, and fraud detection and prevention. A common data lake enables data accessibility and facilitates data sharing, whereby traditional data silos that inhibit analysis and insights are eliminated. A holistic view of data enables AI models to be more accurate and nuanced, leading to better decision-making. Furthermore, the centralization of data into a common data lake simplifies data governance and standards compliance.

6.4 Real-time business events that trigger AI-enabled automated workflows

AI-enabled automated workflows triggered by real-time business events, such as financial transactions, can increase a bank's ability to realize opportunities (e.g., cross-selling) or decrease the bank's ability to avert threats (e.g., fraud). AI models exposed via API are invoked from the workflow engine. Example 1: a high-value transaction can trigger a fraud detection workflow whereby an AI model analyzes the transaction against known fraud patterns, e.g., invoice fraud, and immediately alerts the bank's staff about the suspicious transaction. Example 2: an online loan application can trigger a credit assessment workflow whereby an AI model evaluates the applicant's creditworthiness based on their credit history and other financial status indicators and replies immediately to the applicant with appropriate loan terms. Example 3: a customer complaint or inquiry registered on the bank's website can trigger a case management workflow whereby an AI model using NLP understands the context of the textual dialog, e.g., an account inquiry or service complaint, and provides an immediate personalized response or redirects the case to a bank staff for follow-up.

7 Discussion

7.1 Management implications

Banks must consider several management implications when AI-enabling their back-office operations to maximize benefits while minimizing implementation risks. First, banks must commit to substantial investments in technology as well as staff training and development. Education and awareness programs are essential for bank staff to understand the benefits and limitations of working alongside AI systems. Change management programs are necessary to address staff concerns and perceived threats of job displacement, especially for back-office tasks that are highly repetitive, including staff upskilling and redeployment to higher-value functions. Senior management must be effective in navigating a cultural shift and driving a mindset whereby AI is viewed as a productivity-enhancing tool rather than a replacement.

Since data governance and privacy are a primary concern, banks must ensure that their usage of AI conforms with all applicable data protection laws and ethical standards. This entails handling customer data with care and guaranteeing that it is protected and used transparently. AI integration into existing systems can be challenging, requiring careful planning and a phased implementation approach. Operational risks, such as inaccurate decision-making by AI systems and infrastructure failures, need to be carefully controlled with contingency plans in place.

Bank management must be adaptable and responsive to staff feedback and evolving requirements to continuously assess and modify AI systems. All things considered, a comprehensive management strategy that strikes a balance between technology innovation, people management, operational integrity, and ethical considerations is necessary for the successful integration of AI in back-office operations.

7.2 Maturity model for AI adoption in bank back-office operations

Based on our multiple case studies of four representative banks, we have derived a possible maturity model for assessing banks’ AI adoption in back-office operations, as shown in Fig. 3. The maturity model considers four categories, namely AI benefits (to staff and customers), AI used in back-office operations, AI data pipeline, and AI governance, assessed across four levels of maturity. The assessment objects under each level are only illustrative at this point, and more analysis is needed to refine the model. There may need to be, for example, a different set of assessment objects under the category of “AI use in back-office operations” for each type of bank, e.g., retail, corporate, and investment, as AI use cases may vary for each bank type.

The model has four levels: Level 1: No benefits realized, A I development in experimental stage, Data collection via overnight batch, A I principles, and policies documented. Level 2: 25 percent reduction in back-office staff, A I models in place for common functions, Real-time data sources, A I-enabled workflows, Data privacy and security, and Education and Awareness. Level 3: 50 percent staff reduction, 100 percent increase in transaction volumes, A I models in place for an entire back-office function (retail/corp), On-premises data lake common for all A I model development, and Centre of excellence established for bank-wide A I management. Level 4: 90 percent staff reduction, 200 percent volume increase, Significantly improved customer satisfaction, A I models in place bank-wide for all back-office functions, Full automated ops, Cloud-based data lake, Automated training data split for A I model evaluation and retraining, Explainable A I, Bias mitigation, and Legal and ethical accountability.

In future work, this proposed maturity model can be tested using a self-assessment survey questionnaire to be completed by participating banks. The first round of testing can be done with the four banks studied in this paper, followed by a refinement of the model and/or survey questionnaire, and finally, a second round of testing can be done involving a larger sample set of banks. Once the model is tested and data collected, it may be possible to empirically test hypotheses as to which factors (e.g., technology, people, processes) influence banks’ adoption of AI in back-office operations.

8 Summary

This chapter first examined the generic features of a model digital bank across three tiers of banking needs, namely, retail/SME, wholesale, and investment. These characteristics encompass the absence of physical branches, streamlined customer onboarding, self-service banking transactions, personalized real-time offers, as well as the integration of chatbots and call center support. It was emphasized that each tier tailors the implementation of these generic features according to the specific requirements of customers, regulatory compliance, and operational considerations. Drawing insights from the literature review, the chapter concluded that, in comparison to front and middle offices, AI solutions in the back office have been somewhat lagging. It underscored that banks have predominantly focused on back-office process automation rather than leveraging AI to enhance decision-making within these processes. This chapter subsequently presented the findings from the interviews conducted by the authors on how four banks in SE Asia use AI technology to transform their back-office operations. Based on the analysis of the case studies, this chapter then discussed the various areas where AI can be used in automating back-office operations and the need for a common data pipeline. Finally, this chapter highlighted some of the management implications and proposed a maturity model for guiding the AI adoption in bank back-office operations.
