Chapter 14 AI and Web3 for sustainable digital economy

  1. Feida Zhua
  2. Bingxue Zhangb,c
  3. a Singapore Management University, Singapore, Singapore
  4. b University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, Shanghai, China
  5. c National University of Singapore, Singapore, Singapore

Abstract

This chapter explores the synergies between artificial intelligence (AI) and Web3, emphasizing their combined potential to revolutionize the digital economy. Web3 is defined as a transformative framework for open, decentralized collaboration, emphasizing its role in reshaping the digital economy through collaborative intelligence and tokenized economies. Web3 is no longer just about blockchain but about enabling disruptive changes in technological innovation, legal governance, and economic design. Its ability to facilitate value generation, distribution, and trading of data, intelligence, computational power, and application ecosystems is highlighted as crucial for sustainable development. The chapter explores how Web3’s core pillars—trust and incentive—provide the necessary foundation for secure, transparent, and equitable collaboration in industries like healthcare and finance. AI complements this framework by driving automation and decision-making, but it is Web3 that ensures fairness, privacy, and secure data ownership, creating a new paradigm for collaborative intelligence in an open, decentralized environment. Together, AI and Web3 create a powerful synergy that will drive the future of the digital economy.

Keywords

Web3

Blockchain

Tokenized economy

Decentralized collaboration

Trust and incentive

Collaborative intelligence

1 Introduction

Digital economy is a new economic form that utilizes the digitized knowledge and information as a key production factor, the digital technology as a core driving force, and the modern information network as an important carrier [1]. It comprises four main parts: (1) Digital industrialization: It refers to the information and communication industry, especially the software and technological services. (2) Industry digitization: It refers to the value growth brought by the application of digital technology in traditional industries, e.g., platform economy and internet of vehicles. (3) Digital governance: It includes digital public services or the industries that establish their governance systems combined with digital technology. (4) Data valorization: It covers the data collection, data pricing, data transactions, and other activities. Currently, the digital economy has emerged as a pivotal force propelling global economic growth. According to the report of the World Bank, the digital economy makes up more than 15% of the global GDP and has grown 2.5 times faster over the previous 10 years than the GDP of the physical world [2].

However, as the scale of the digital economy continuously expands, traditional data processing and management methods can no longer meet the emerging needs. Especially, the challenges in intelligence, automation, and security have become increasingly prominent. Therefore, exploring the new technologies that can support the sustainable development of the digital economy has become the research and work priority. In this context, artificial intelligence (AI) and Web3 technologies show great potential.

  1. (1) AI empowers the digital economy with intelligence and automation: New analysis technologies represented by AI are based on the collection and analysis of massive data, which not only significantly improves production efficiency and intelligence, but also profoundly changes the decision-making patterns. It plays a vital role in various areas of the digital economy, including providing personalized services, content creation, detecting potential fraud, and optimizing user experience.
  2. (2) Web3 catalyzes the digital economy rooted in data value and mutual trust: Web3, based on blockchain, endeavors to construct a decentralized, zero-trust, secure, and autonomous network paradigm. It puts data ownership first. Through a series of innovative concepts such as decentralized identity (DID), nonfungible token (NFT), decentralized autonomous organization (DAO), and decentralized finance (DeFi), Web3 pioneers a new economic system for the data elements with authentication, circulation, and trading in the digital world.
    Therefore, applying AI and Web3 technology to the digital economy can not only optimize the existing business models of digital economy, but also foster the emergence of novel commercial paradigms and innovative forms. Consequently, this will promote the sustainable development of the digital economy. In this chapter, we will explore how AI and Web3 empower the digital economy and analyze their impact on the future development of digital economy.

2 The development of digital economy powered by big data and AI

The rapid advancement of digital economy owes much to the driving forces of big data and AI technology. The value of big data lies in its excellent data processing and analysis capabilities, which serve as the essential fuel for AI's intelligent decision-making. The value of AI is rooted in its ability to learn and mimic human thinking and decision-making processes, and then provide automated solutions and innovative services. These two technologies have not only transformed the business models and service modes of digital economy, but also engendered the unprecedented value across numerous industries.

2.1 The ubiquity of big data

2.1.1 Introduction of big data

Big data refers to datasets that are vast in volume, diverse in type, rapid in growth speed, and exceed the processing capabilities of traditional database technologies. The prominent characteristics of big data can be summarized within the “5Vs” framework [3]: volume, velocity, variety, veracity, and value. The details are as follows.

  • • Volume: The sheer amount of data is immense, and typically exceeds terabytes (TB) or petabytes (PB).
  • • Velocity: The speed of data generation and accumulation is very fast, and has high requirements on data processing speed.
  • • Variety: The data types cover a wide variety, including structured, semistructured, and unstructured data.
  • • Veracity: The data possess a high degree of credibility and accuracy.
  • • Value: The data hold tremendous potential for value extraction.

The earlier 5Vs characteristics constitute the core value of big data. Through the analysis and mining of big data, more deep-seated patterns and trends can be revealed. It can provide powerful data support and accurate decision-making assistance for various industrial fields within the digital economy.

2.1.2 Digital economy powered by big data

In the digital economy, data represents not only the core asset, but also the basis for innovation and value creation. Big data technology plays a pivotal role across various sectors within the digital economy and deeply integrates many key industries such as financial technology, e-commerce, and digital health. It injects the “fuel” into the intelligent development of the digital economy, and accelerates the growth of digital transformation technologies like AI, Internet of Things, and cloud computing. It provides the powerful data support and intelligent guidance for decision-making processes in the digital economy. Big data brings an important value enhancement to the digital economic environment.

  1. (1) Data-driven transformation of decision-making patterns: The core value of big data lies in its ability to reveal the underlying information and patterns through in-depth analysis of massive and complex datasets. This capacity has moved away from the traditional economic industries’ decision-making patterns that rely on subjective experience and intuition. The digital economy industries can significantly enhance the accuracy and efficiency of decision-making, thereby empowering various digital economy industries to achieve optimized strategic planning and allocation.
  2. (2) Optimizing business modes through data mining: In the context of the digital economy, the companies can leverage real-time data monitoring systems to improve the accuracy of risk predictions and optimize risk management. Besides, the companies can accurately uncover the differences in consumers’ preferences and behaviors through in-depth analysis of massive data from social media, search engines, online shopping platforms, etc. This insight enables the targeted adjustment of product development and market positioning to adapt to shifts in consumer needs and market changes. Take Netflix as an example, by decoding the viewing patterns of users’ viewing habits, it powers the real-time recommendations and guides the content creation and purchasing decisions. Consequently, the pace of investment was greatly accelerated, culminating in resounding business success [4].
  3. (3) Revolutionization of data processing capabilities: We are witnessing an exponential surge in data volumes in the digital economy. The application of big data technology has greatly enhanced the data processing capabilities and significantly transformed the efficiency of industrial operations. For instance, the emergence of in-memory computing framework—Spark [5] breaks through the speed limitations of Disk I/O, fulfilling the need for rapid processing and analysis of massive data. The use of data lake architecture [6] has increased the flexibility and scalability of processing the structured and unstructured data, enabling the digital economy industries to be compatible with more heterogeneous data. In addition, the digital economy industry can utilize data visualization tools, such as Google Data Studio [7], to graphically present the complex and abstract data analytical results, which significantly improves the decision-makers’ and users’ intuitive insights into data, and swiftly identifying the patterns, trends as well as recognizing the exceptions from data. These advancements in digital economy have not only improved the efficiency and accuracy of data processing, but also provided possibilities for the companies to capture immediate market opportunities, and empower the development of digital economy.

2.2 The boom of AI

2.2.1 Introduction of Al

Artificial intelligence (AI) refers to the technical and scientific domain that enables machines to emulate human intelligence processes, covering core functions such as learning, inference, and self-correction. Recent advancements in AI technology, especially within the domains of deep learning and reinforcement learning, have shown great performance and potential across diverse application scenarios. For example, computer vision(CV) technology empowers the computers to parse the visual information, facilitating the extraction and recognition of image information, which provides substantial technical support for medical diagnosis, parcel sorting, and other fields; natural language processing (NLP) technology, through the textual comprehension and sentiment analysis, enables computers to process, understand and generate human language. It is widely applied in the scenarios like chat robots and machine translation. Speech recognition technology can convert human speech into machine-readable formats, laying the groundwork for applications like voice assistants and voice interaction systems. Meanwhile, expert system, by simulating the expert's decision-making abilities and integrating expert's knowledge base to infer and solve related professional problems, has achieved commendable application results in fields like financial analysis and smart education.

Currently, large language model (LLM) is setting the stage for a revolutionary era, with internationally renowned companies actively developing LLM-based applications. OpenAI has released the GPT4 [8], a multimodal pretraining model with hundreds of billions of parameters. Through cooperation with Microsoft and open GPT4 plug-ins, OpenAI has built a multiindustry application ecosystem. For instance, by integrating with Microsoft office software, the office productivity can be greatly boosted; by connecting with Github, the code generation based on natural language can be realized [9]. In addition, OpenAI has also launched the text-to-video model—Sora [10], which can generate high-quality videos by inputting text. Google has released PaLM2 [11], a rival to GPT, which excels in multilanguage translation. IBM released Watsonx [12], featuring functionalities such as automated business processes and AI governance.

2.2.2 Digital economy powered by AI

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technology into digital economy is universally regarded as a catalyst for economic expansion and industrial upgrading. Insights from Riley's research suggest that AI technology is instrumental in transforming traditional economic industries by improving production efficiency and enhancing industrial intelligence and service quality [13]. AI can automatically process and analyze data and predict trends based on data, effectively improving industrial competitiveness. For example, the application of AI in customer service, fraud detection, risk assessment, supply chain optimization, personalized marketing, content creation, and product development empowers the intelligent transformation of various industries in the digital economy environment.

  1. (1) Tailored marketing strategies: By leveraging deep learning technology, companies or organizations can provide customized services and products tailored to user behaviors and preferences, significantly improving user experience and market competitiveness. Consider Spotify's personalized recommendation algorithm, it can recommend personalized music playlists to users by analyzing their listening history and behavior patterns. AI-recommended songs have accounted for 30% of Spotify's traffic, and users engage with the platform an average of 61 times per month, thus significantly increasing the user stickiness and subscription rate [14].
  2. (2) Multimodal content creation: In the field of digital content creation, AI has the capability to automatically generate content across various modalities, such as text, images, and videos. It greatly improved the efficiency and quality of digital content creation, and significantly reduced the creation costs. For example, the creators can utilize ChatGPT to quickly generate promotional text or employ Sora for creating cinematic special effects, which can substantially enhance the creation efficiency and innovation. What once took several days or even months to complete can now be effortlessly accomplished in just a few minutes. It can pave the way for the diversity of digital contents.
  3. (3) Personalized customer service: In the digital economy, AI-driven chatbots have brought about a revolutionary enhancement to customer service. It can enable 24/7 instant response that significantly improves the user experience and effectively reduces the operational costs for businesses. In addition, the intelligent search engines, exemplified by NewBing's adoption of natural language processing technology [15], allow users to perform content retrieval and Q&A interactions in natural language, thereby obtaining their required information more intuitively and efficiently.
  4. (4) Supply chain optimization: In terms of supply chain management, the application of AI can not only optimize inventory management and reduce inventory management costs, but also improve the transparency and response speed of the supply chain through efficient logistics planning. For instance, Zara has utilized AI to optimize supply chain management, and its new design ensures the delivery within just 1 week—a stark contrast to the industry average speed of 3–6 months. It also improves delivery accuracy and minimizes inventory costs, significantly boosting customer satisfaction [16].
  5. (5) Automated fraud detection and risk assessment: The AI-powered risk and security management provides a solid safeguard for the development of the digital economy. The AI-based fraud detection system is capable of monitoring and analyzing the transaction data in real-time, effectively preventing the financial fraud and network attacks, and protecting the user funds. For instance, according to the Visa report, the AI-driven fraud detection implemented in 2023 resulted in a 45% decrease in fraudulent transactions and a 60% decrease in fraud losses compared to the previous year [17].

To sum up, AI technology plays a vital role in the development of digital economy. It not only optimizes the operational efficiency and decision-making quality of the digital economic industry, but also drives the innovations in services and products. Moreover, it has provided a strong safeguard for the security of economic activities. With the ongoing advancements in AI technology and the expansion of application fields, its value in the digital economy is set to become even more pronounced, which can promote the high-quality development of the digital economy.

3 The challenges of today's digital economy

With the widespread application of big data and AI technology in the digital economy, there have been significant improvements in efficiency and industrial transformation, yet some challenges that remain to be addressed.

3.1 Challenges for data

  1. (1) Challenges in data security and privacy: In the era of digital economy, data contains a wealth of sensitive information such as personal privacy, and business secrets. It faces the challenges of security threats and privacy leaks in data transmission, storage, and processing stage. To address these challenges, academia and industry have proposed possible solution strategies for each stage, including data transmission, storage, and processing. In the data transmission phase, the technologies such as cross-domain secure exchange and SSL encryption protocol aim to provide a secure transmission channel, ensuring data confidentiality and integrity during transmission. In the data storage stage, some studies utilize use cryptography technology under distributed storage (e.g., cryptographic service cluster key dynamic configuration management), storage isolation, access control, redundant backup, and other technologies to secure the data while enhancing its fault tolerance and recoverability. In the data processing stage, through the mechanisms like secure multiparty computation (e.g., homomorphic encryption [18], secret sharing), the sensitive data stored in ciphertext state can be efficiently computed without revealing its plaintexts. Through the comprehensive application of the earlier strategies, the risk of data being attacked at various stages can be effectively reduced.
  2. (2) Challenges in complexity of data fusion: In the context of the digital economy, a flourishing range of data sources has emerged with immense diversity, including image data, audio data, video data, text data, and other heterogeneous data formats, each associated with different business scenarios like finance, healthcare, and social networking. In this way, a vast and intricate data collection will be formed. With the increasing diversity of data sources, how to effectively integrate these heterogeneous data generated in the digital economy has become a key challenge. Faced with this challenge, the researchers have begun to explore possible strategies for data fusion, such as Polyglot data stores [19], which leverage multiple data storage technologies to meet the storage demands of different data types, providing fresh perspectives to surmount the difficulties of data fusion.
  3. (3) Challenges in data governance: The development of the digital economy has intensified the complexity of data governance, involving not only the clear demarcation of data ownership but also a series of legal and jurisdictional issues over cross-border data flows. In response to these problems, the researchers have begun to consider related strategies for digital governance. For example, the scholar Elouataoui proposed that implementing the effective metadata management is a potential resolution [20]. It helps clarify the management responsibilities and data usage by providing clear definitions, attributions, access rights, and usage specifications for the data elements. This approach not only enhances data transparency, but also promotes the standardization and normalization of data governance. In addition, the governance of cross-border and cross-organization data has become a new research direction that calls for establishing robust legal frameworks and ensuring that the cross-border data flow complies with the requirements of local laws and regulations.
  4. (4) Challenges in real-time processing of massive data: In the digital economy, an abundance of real-time transactions will be generated, accompanied by an increasing demand for the real-time processing of massive data. This requires the data processing system to be able to act in response and process the high-speed influx of data to maintain efficient operations. In this regard, academia and industry have proposed a series of strategies. For instance, data stream processing and large-scale data dissemination technologies, e.g., Apache Kafka [21] and Flink [22], have been developed to optimize the real-time processing and dissemination mechanism of data. It provides critical support for real-time transaction processing and analysis. The application of these technologies plays a positive role in ensuring the efficient operation of the digital economic system and provides valuable solutions for the real-time processing of massive data.

3.2 Challenges for AI

With AI technology integrating into digital economic activities, a series of challenges have emerged as follows.

  1. (1) Challenges in the bias and discrimination of AI: In the field of digital economy, AI systems are extensively applied to consumer analysis, credit scoring, human resources, and other fields. However, during the training and inference processes, AI often incorporates human biases, which may lead to unfair treatment of certain groups, especially in online advertising, credit approval, recruitment, and other domains. How to ensure the fairness of the AI system and avoid generating potentially discriminatory content is a significant challenge faced by AI in digital economy. To address this challenge, enhancing data diversity is a potential solution that can help prevent AI from favoring certain groups due to data imbalance. Additionally, the fairness assessment frameworks (such as AI Fairness 360 [23]) and algorithm auditing techniques can detect and mitigate the unfairness of AI models, and recognize and quantify the potential biases in AI model decision-making, which can help to prevent and eliminate the discrimination issues caused by the AI model.
  2. (2) Challenges in explainability and transparency of AI decision-making: As AI's application in the digital economy field becomes increasingly widespread, the users are demanding greater explainability and transparency of AI decision-making. In digital economy applications such as automated financial analysis and digital healthcare, the “black box” nature of AI systems makes it difficult for professionals to trust their decisions. For example, when the results provided by the AI healthcare system are at odds with the medical professionals’ initial judgment and lack explanatory support, the users will have difficulty understanding and trusting the AI's decision-making. To tackle this challenge, developing explainable AI (XAI) models [24] presents a feasible approach. The XAI model aims to make the AI decision-making process more transparent to users, offering clarity on the underlying logic and inference, and thus bolstering users’ trust in the AI systems.
  3. (3) Challenges in privacy leakage of AI: In the digital economy sector, intelligent services are contingent on AI's processing and analysis of user data. However, if the user data collected by the AI service provider is used for unintended purposes, or is attacked by untrustworthy computing participants during the AI training process, it will pose a serious threat to users’ personal privacy and data security. How to provide personalized AI services while ensuring the privacy and security of user data is a major challenge in the development of AI. To solve this challenge, the comprehensive application of diverse privacy computing strategies is required. For example, encrypting user data during transmission and combining with secure multiparty computation like garbled circuit, secret sharing, and homomorphic encryption, and combining hardware enhancement methods like trust executive environment [25] can safeguard the computational privacy of user data during AI training and inference phase. Besides, the research on data separation-based privacy protection strategies (e.g., hybrid cloud detached execution, federated learning [26]), and data interference-based privacy protection strategies (e.g., differential privacy [27], data anonymity) can further enhance the confidentiality of user data.

4 The history and rise of Web3

4.1 The evolution of Web3

The evolution of Web3 signifies the progressive development of internet technology. From the Web 1.0 era's one-directional information dissemination, through the Web 2.0 era's interactive participation and content creation by users, culminating in the Web 3.0 era. It heralds a significant shift in the control rights and data ownership for users [28]. The details are as follows.

In the Web 1.0 era, web content production was platform-centric, which is characterized by the one-directional flow of information. The user was primarily confined to the role of recipient. Typically, they can only click on the links on the webpage to browse the text, pictures, and other content predetermined by the developers. Users were essentially the viewers, lacking the opportunities for participation and interaction.

With the advent of Web 2.0, users have transformed into content creators and promoted the diversified development of the content through interaction and cooperation on social media platforms. However, although the content creation rights are transferred to users, the data ownership and control rights are still concentrated in the hands of the platform owners.

Entering the Web 3.0 era, underpinned by the blockchain technology, users are not just the creators of the content, but also its owners and enjoy the value it generates, which can promote the construction of a more secure, trustworthy, and fair digital economic ecosystem.

4.2 The composition of Web3

As the digital economy's influence on global economic activities expands, the value of digital assets also rises. On one hand, the traditional forms of assets, like currencies or commodities have found new value anchors in the digital field, achieving the circulation and trading capabilities in the digital environment. On the other hand, society's gradual adoption of digital culture has also bolstered the valuation of new assets such as digital certificates, digital artworks, virtual lands, and game props.

Web3 leverages the blockchain as its underpinning technology to build a value network centered around the digital assets. It encompasses two core value propositions: decentralization and tokenization. From the perspective of decentralization, Web3 emphasizes that the users have ownership over their personal data, and ensures that they can realize the transactions and interactions without trusting any specific parties. It also highlights the vision of openness and co-construction. It advocates that internet application services should be sufficiently open in terms of technology, data, algorithm, etc., and should enable the ordinary users to engage in every aspect of internet application service, including production, exchange, and consumption. From the standpoint of tokenization, Web3 highlights the importance of value circulation, positing that digital property rights in the digital space can circulate swiftly. The data and contents created by users can be mapped into various digitalized tokens through tokenization. It greatly facilitates the data authentication, data transactions, data transfer, and other applications in the form of digital token circulation. Web3 plays a key role in empowering the development of the digital economy and provides new models and paths for digital economic activities through a series of innovative concepts, such as decentralized identity (DID) [29], decentralized finance (DeFi) [30], nonfungibility tokens (NFT) [31], decentralized applications (DApps) [32], and decentralized autonomous organizations (DAO) [33]. The details are as follows.

  • • DID (Decentralized identity): DID allows individuals or organizations to establish and manage their own identity information without relying on any centralized organization, ensuring the security of identity information. This underpins the trust and secure trading in the digital economy and paves the way for the establishment of digital identity and reputation systems.
  • • DeFi (Decentralized finance): DeFi leverages smart contracts to create financial tools on the blockchain. It can realize the lending, trading, and management of assets without the traditional financial intermediaries like banks or stock exchanges. This greatly expands the coverage of financial services and increases the accessibility of the financial market.
  • • NFT (Nonfungible token): NFT is a digital token representing the unique asset. Based on blockchain technology, the indivisibility, nontampering, and nonreplicability of each NFT will be guaranteed. NFT represents ownership and authenticity of a unique asset like digital collectibles, virtual lands, and game props, carving out a new value market for content creators and collectors.
  • • DApp (Decentralized applications): DApp is an open-source application running in a decentralized manner. It uses smart contracts to define and execute the rules and logic, covering a wide range of categories, like social media platforms and games, which can greatly meet the users’ diverse needs in the digital economy.
  • • DAO (Decentralized autonomous organization): DAO is an organizational form based on smart contracts. Through code execution management and decision-making, DAO can achieve fully decentralized decision-making and resource allocation. This empowers the community members to participate in project and platform development management.

The integration of the above-mentioned Web3 technology with the digital economy can significantly accelerate the diversification of the digital economy and foster a shift toward a decentralized paradigm. Web3 not only grants the users control over their data and online identities, but also infuses the digital assets with newfound significance. It drives the emergence of new economic platforms with digital autonomy and trust. Therefore, Web3 is endowed with the milestone significance in the development of digital economy, symbolizing that the economic system is evolving in a more open, secure, and user-led direction.

4.3 Challenges for Web3

  1. (1) Challenges in transaction efficiency and cost: The rise of digital economic applications necessitates the capacities to process large-scale and real-time data. One of the key challenges the Web3 technology faces is its relatively low transaction efficiency and high transaction cost. Compared to traditional centralized Web2 applications, Web3 falls short in data processing efficiency. The increase in user base and transaction volume leads to network congestion and increase in transaction fees. To deal with these issues, researchers are actively exploring the solutions, including sharding technology, off-chain computing, and Layer2 solutions [34] (such as state channels, sidechains, Plasma) to improve transaction throughput while preserving system security.
  2. (2) Challenges in user privacy protection: In the data-driven digital economy, privacy protection is a new challenge faced by Web3. The decentralized nature of Web3 enhances the data security and censorship resistance. However, due to the transparency mechanism of the blockchain, it may expose sensitive user data that should not be public, which poses new privacy protection challenges. For this reason, it is crucial for developing efficient privacy protection technologies, such as secure multiparty computation, and zero-knowledge proof [35], which can perform data processing, transactions, and verification without leaking users’ privacy.
  3. (3) Challenges in interoperability: The diversity of the digital economic applications has led to a situation where various project teams need to build their own infrastructure, resulting in the lack of coordination. It has brought about the new issues such as the high cost of new chain construction and low interoperability efficiency. This restricts the interconnectivity among different platforms and technologies and also erects the barriers for the users in accessing assets and services across different platforms. Efforts are underway, by developing cross-chain technology and improving standardized protocols, the researchers are working to facilitate the circulation of data assets among different blockchains, enhancing the interoperability among various DApps and improving the connectivity of the digital economy.
  4. (4) Challenges in governance and supervision: The digital economy involves a wide range of asset transactions requiring market fairness and the protection of consumer rights. Since the decentralized nature of Web3 is contrary to the traditional regulatory approaches, it adds complexity to the governance and supervision of the digital economy. For example, it is difficult to define the regulatory subjects. Besides, according to the decentralized governance mechanism, the DAO members’ arbitrary joining and leaving have also contributed to regulatory instability. Addressing these challenges calls for the continuous improvement of laws, regulations, and governance mechanisms, and promotes the formulation of new rules that adapt to digital assets and decentralized services.

Despite facing the challenges in transaction efficiency, cost, privacy protection, interoperability, governance, etc., the Web3’s role in the digital economy will be increasingly significant. The continuous technological and institutional improvements are expected to overcome existing challenges. In the future, with the further integration of technologies such as the Internet of Things, and AI, Web3 is expected to play an increasingly important role in improving the user experience, from online identity and data ownership to financial transactions and web governance, driving the ongoing innovation of the digital economy.

5 Why the marriage between AI and Web3

5.1 Collaborative intelligence and the future of computing

The trajectory of computing is moving toward a ubiquitous and collaborative future. In this future, data, intelligence, computational power, and the application ecosystem must collaborate to create value greater than the sum of its parts. The era of isolated systems and siloed datasets is coming to an end, and a new paradigm, which we term “Collaborative Intelligence,” is emerging.

Collaborative Intelligence is a framework in which various actors—from individuals to large enterprises—contribute their data, computing resources, and models to collaboratively train machine learning systems. In this ecosystem, all parties benefit from each other's input and expertise. Model training becomes a collective endeavor, leveraging decentralized knowledge and intelligence. This decentralization introduces efficiency and innovation across various domains, but it requires a strong foundation of trust and incentives for collaboration to flourish.

5.2 The need for trust and incentives in collaboration

In a highly collaborative environment like the one described, the interaction between various actors must be governed by two fundamental components: Trust and Incentive.

Trust is necessary to ensure that all parties in the system can interact without fear of malicious behavior, data theft, or manipulation. It creates an environment where shared resources—be they data or computational power—are secure and used for mutual benefit.

Incentives, on the other hand, ensure that all contributing parties are adequately rewarded for their participation in the collaborative framework. Whether in terms of profit, access to enhanced systems, or other forms of value generation, participants must be motivated to contribute and collaborate in a fair and structured way.

These two components form the backbone of any collaborative intelligence system and are essential for its success. However, artificial intelligence (AI) alone cannot provide or enforce these components.

While trust and incentives are essential to foster collaboration, it is equally important to recognize that AI alone cannot govern these aspects effectively. This limitation underscores the need for a decentralized framework that Web3 provides, where collaboration can be securely managed and fairly rewarded.

By definition, AI is a tool designed for specific tasks—from pattern recognition to predictive analysis—but it lacks the capability to govern the socioeconomic dimensions of collaboration.

Take, for example, the case of five hospitals that wish to collaborate on training a machine learning model for diagnosing a particular disease. Each hospital alone does not possess sufficient data to train an effective model, but by pooling their datasets, they stand a much better chance of success. Suppose this collaboration leads to the development of a highly profitable AI model. The question arises: how should the profits be distributed among the hospitals? How should each party's contribution be valued?

These are complex governance and economic questions that lie beyond the scope of AI. AI can build the model, but it cannot fairly allocate resources and rewards or ensure transparency in collaboration. These issues require a different framework — one that Web3 is uniquely positioned to address.

5.3 Defining Web3: A framework for open, decentralized collaboration

We define Web3 as the totality of disruptive changes in technological innovation, legal governance, economic design, and business models required to enable value generation, distribution, sharing, and trading. These changes focus on four core elements: data, intelligence, computational power, and the application ecosystem, all in an open, decentralized yet collaborative setting.

Web3 fundamentally reimagines the internet, replacing centralized, trust-based systems with decentralized protocols where collaboration and value exchange occur without reliance on traditional intermediaries. The key innovation in Web3 is the ability to tokenize various forms of value, turning them into computable objects that can be shared, traded, and allocated in a transparent and decentralized manner.

As Web3 redefines the way we approach collaboration and governance, its core strength lies in combining collaborative intelligence with tokenized economies. These innovations transform the value-generation process and enable decentralized systems to operate efficiently and transparently.

In simple terms, Web3 can be thought of as the convergence of Collaborative Intelligence and a Tokenized Economy. Collaborative intelligence represents the means of generating value by pooling decentralized resources, while the tokenized economy captures, distributes, and reallocates this value. Through tokenization, the contributions of different actors can be quantified, and incentives can be tied directly to these computable tokens.

Tokenized value exchange systems, such as cryptocurrencies and other digital assets, allow for the seamless integration of incentive structures into collaborative intelligence frameworks.

5.4 The two core pillars of Web3: Trust and incentive

The foundation of Web3 relies on two core pillars: Trust and Incentive. Each of these pillars is essential to fostering the decentralized collaboration that Web3 enables.

5.4.1 The trust pillar

Trust in Web3 is established through several critical components:

  • • Trusted Computing-Based Secure Data Binding
    Ensuring secure and verifiable data sharing across decentralized systems is vital. Mechanisms such as hashing functions and asymmetric encryption provide data integrity, ensuring that data is not tampered with and remains secure.
  • • Decentralized Computing-Based Data Consistency and Storage
    In decentralized systems, data consistency and integrity must be maintained. Consensus protocols, such as those used in blockchain networks, ensure that distributed ledgers reflect the same data across all nodes, thereby eliminating discrepancies.
  • • Open-Code-Based Transparency and Executability
    Transparency is a cornerstone of trust in Web3. Open-source code ensures that smart contracts—self-executing programs that automate transactions based on predefined conditions—are publicly auditable and tamperresistant.
  • • Privacy-Enhancing Computation
    Data privacy is of paramount importance in collaborative intelligence. Techniques like differential privacy, federated learning, and zero-knowledge proofs ensure that sensitive data can be used for model training or analysis without revealing private information.
  • • Fairness
    Ensuring fairness in data collaboration includes mechanisms for fair data pricing, data auditing, and equitable sharing of rewards among participants.

5.4.2 The incentive pillar

The incentive pillar enables value creation, distribution, and capture in the Web3 ecosystem through several components:

  • • Data and AI Assetization
    Data and AI models can be tokenized, transforming them into tradable assets. There are two primary types of tokens: fungible tokens, which represent standardized value, and nonfungible tokens (NFTs), which represent unique assets. Tokenomics designs involve creating incentive structures, including mechanism design, market design, and price determination to facilitate asset trading.
  • • Interoperability
    Web3 enables the interaction of different financial systems, such as decentralized finance (DeFi), social finance (SocialFi), and game finance (GameFi). Various models, like “X-to-earn,” allow for the creation of novel incentive mechanisms tied to real-world activities.
  • • Secure Asset Management
    Security is paramount in managing on-chain assets. Tools for on-chain data analytics, wallet security, cross-chain security, and custody security ensure that digital assets remain protected. Additionally, smart contract auditing ensures that the underlying code governing tokenized assets is secure and free of vulnerabilities.

5.5 Advances in key assetization technologies: Data auditing

With the rising awareness of data assetization, data governance, which is to understand where data comes from, how it is collected, and how it is used, has been assuming ever-growing importance. One critical component of data governance gaining increasing attention is auditing machine learning models to determine if specific data has been used for training. In this section, we introduce the advances in data auditing as a key assetization technology.

In an era of accelerated digital transformation, data has been widely recognized as an emerging asset class. In particular, with the rise and sweeping adoption of large models such as GPT-4 [36] and DALL-E [37], the competition in business intelligence has shifted from the design of the ML model to the curation of proprietary data. As a result, understanding where data comes from, how it is collected, and how it can be best used, etc., known as data governance [38,39], has been assuming ever-increasing importance. It provides insight into the sources and history of data, enabling better decision-making and ensuring responsible use of data assets.

Within the domain of data governance, there is a critical component that has attracted considerable attention from both academia and industry: Auditing Data Provenance (ADP), i.e., how to audit if a given piece of data (which will be referred to as auditing data for the rest of this paper) has been used for training a target machine learning model [40–42]. With the booming of IoT, 5G and large language models, data intelligence in the future is bound to be collaborative in nature—models could potentially be trained with data from various sources and domains in data marketplaces or other coordinated settings, e.g., federated learning, and generate real revenue that needs to be attributed to all data contributors. The motivations for ADP, while varying by applications, are therefore manifested most prominently by two critical aspects—(I) Privacy and (II) Incentive governance. Let's examine an example for each scenario: (I) Privacy: Imagine a user's data has been collected and used to train a machine learning model without her knowledge. To protect her data privacy, an objectively rigorous and quantifiable auditing method is necessary to substantiate her challenge in potential disputes. (II) Incentive governance: In a setting where multiple parties each contribute and trade data to collectively train models in a collaborative manner, e.g., federated learning in a decentralized variant in which no central nodes are commanding incentivization [43]. The incentive allocation in such a scenario would necessarily entail auditing the usage of all parties’ data to a sufficiently fine granularity to achieve trust and fairness.

From a taxonomy point of view, there are two directions for this problem: One direction is based on model-specific techniques. One example along this direction is to directly audit the target model's training process. Techniques, such as regularization and data augmentation which “memorize” information about the training data set in the model, have been proposed without compromising the performance of the model [44]. Unfortunately, most real auditing settings allow access only to the output or the final parameters of the target model, rather than the training process itself. Another example is to directly design a criterion on the model output to compare training data and nontraining data with a preset threshold, e.g., the prediction loss [45] or the prediction confidence (e.g., class probability) [46]. Methods along this line suffer from limited generality due to their reliance on specific criteria.

An alternative research direction is based on a shadow training technique, which has demonstrated successful application in auditing deep learning models [40,41]. The main idea is to use multiple “shadow models” to imitate the behavior of the target model. As the training data for the shadow models are known, the target model can be trained using the labeled outputs of the shadow models. While the shadow training technique is promising for a number of scenarios, it raises two technical challenges:

  • • Shadow model generation. The creation of shadow models entails two necessary requirements: (I) The knowledge of the training protocol for the target model; and (II) The generation of training data for shadow models. Requirement (I) is not always guaranteed in real applications. Requirement (II) means it is necessary to generate multiple data sets based on some heuristic rules.
  • • Cumulative errors. The final auditing results depend on multiple intermediate results of machine learning models. It may cause uncertainties in practice as error accumulates.

In [47], a different approach is adopted by leveraging the following observations: In general, a machine learning model tends to fit the training data well with a relatively high confidence, as, after all, the model has witnessed these data. If we apply a carefully designed function, i.e., auditing function, to transform both the training and nontraining data before feeding them as input to the target model respectively, the training data side would result in a much greater difference in the target model's output between the original input data and the transformed one. This difference in the confidence of the target model's output between training and nontraining data is identified as the key to the DPDA auditing framework proposed in this paper. As illustrated in Fig. 1, the auditing framework is constituted by introducing an auditing function, which would be applied to the auditing data before feeding into the target model in one path of the comparison.

The diagram shows two main processes. The first process starts with a cylinder labeled Auditing data leading to a rectangle labeled Target Model, which then leads to another rectangle labeled Output. The second process starts with a cube labeled Auditing Function containing a cylinder labeled Auditing data, leading to a rectangle labeled Target Model, which then leads to another rectangle labeled Output. Both outputs are connected to a label Differential Function. On the right side, there is a graph with axes labeled Differential and 0. The graph contains two ovals labeled Training and Non-Training with a gradient scale next to them.

Based on this framework, authors in [47] propose two implementations, an additive implementation (DPDA-ADD) and a multiplicative implementation (DPDA-MUL). DPDA-ADD applies additive transfer functions on input data to generate statistically significant differences, i.e., the changes in model output on training data are more significant than on nontraining data. Such additive transfer functions can be easily obtained by maximizing the prediction error of the target model. DPDA-MUL uses a projection function to more carefully emphasize the differential between the training and nontraining data, which can be learned by an alternative optimization technique to bridge the auditing model and the target model.

The proposed framework differs from the above-mentioned approaches in two key aspects. First, unlike the model-specific method, the proposed framework does not rely on specific model output, it can therefore be applied to a wider range of applications to multiple target models. Second, unlike the shadow-based method which learns a combination of multiple shadow models to simulate the target model, the proposed framework derives a data transformed directly from data through one auditing function, and the mechanism for auditing function is simpler than all these shadow-based approaches.

Another fundamentally important issue re-examined in [47] is the granularity of data that should be the subject of auditing [48]. The authors argue that what should be used is the notion of group-based data auditing where a set of data points collectively exhibit the characteristics of training or nontraining data because it reflects better the auditing needs of real applications. For example, in applications where a model has been trained with users’ facial images or text sets (e.g., tweets), the real question that matters is whether a particular user's data has been used in the training, rather than whether a particular image or tweet of the user has been used. A model should be judged to have already used a user's data if a subset sufficiently characteristic of the user has indeed been used, even if some individual data points are left out in the training.

6 Advances in key application context

This section is an abstract and extension of “Managing Metaverse Data Tsunami: Actionable Insights”, co-authored by Bingxue ZHANG, one of the authors of this book.

6.1 Metaverse

Traditionally, the physical space and the virtual space are disjoint and distinct. Users in each space operate within the scope of the space, i.e., they may communicate among themselves but do not cross the boundary to the other space. However, technological advances in hardware (e.g., GPUs, FPGAs, NVM), Internet of Things (IoT), 5G [49], artificial intelligence, blockchain, smart interfaces, and new augmented realities have made it possible for these two spaces to co-exist within a unified space, namely, the metaverse.

In a recent investment report [50], it is projected that “the metaverse represents a potential 8𝓉𝓇𝒾𝓁𝓁𝒾ℴ𝓃𝓉ℴ 13 trillion opportunity by 2030, that could boast as many as 5 billion users.” Companies such as Meta and Microsoft are already investing a significant amount of resources in the metaverse.

In the metaverse, we can design innovative applications that provide experiences and opportunities that neither the physical nor the virtual spaces can offer. Some example applications include location-based games and social networking, partnership in shopping among online and physical shoppers, and enhanced digital models that capture physical troop movements.

Within such a context, it is easy to see that a large amount of data and information must flow within the metaverse and between the real and virtual spaces to ensure that the two worlds are synchronized. This brings new challenges such as a need to process heterogeneous data streams to materialize real-world events in the virtual world and to disseminate information about interesting events in the virtual space to users in the physical world. In addition, new technologies are needed to enable users to manage information seamlessly between the real and digital spaces. These include AI, smart interfaces, blockchain, efficient storage management, and large-scale data dissemination.

In this chapter, we present two promising data-rich metaverse applications. Then we analyze how AI and blockchain can empower the metaverse applications and come up with several challenges for applying the two technologies from the perspective of data.

6.1.1 The marketplace

In today's marketplace, we either shop in a mall or buy our products online. A physical shop may have a web page (a very primitive form of the virtual model), but there is very limited real-time interaction between the two spaces.

In tomorrow's metaverse shop, a physical space may be “expanded” to display more items. Similarly, in tomorrow's metaverse marketplace, a physical mall will be “expanded” into a mall (virtually) that houses many more shops than the physical mall. In addition to the virtual correspondence of the physical shops, the virtual mall can rent out virtual space for virtual shop owners. In the physical mall, screens (large displays) can be set up within each physical shop for cyber shoppers to communicate with physical shoppers within the same shop (e.g., through simple text messages and/or more sophisticated immersive technologies). While a physical shopper is restricted to the shops that are physically located in the mall, the online shopper has a wider selection of shops (and products). The virtual mall needs to be kept up-to-date with real-time information from the physical mall, e.g., live programs that are happening in the physical mall, ongoing lucky draws, and updates on the availability of products. The same concept may be used to “expand” the space for exhibits in a museum, or even “expand” a stadium's sitting capacity for the global audience: sports enthusiasts may view a game through the “eyes” of the player, and concert audiences may have a close-up immersive experience.

The AI-empowered metaverse will become the game changer for traditional production and consumption phenomenon. In today's marketplace, the manufacturers need to design and produce the products in advance, which often results in overproduction and inability to sell the products. In tomorrow's marketplace, as shown in Fig. 2, the sellers can use AI technology to generate plenty of virtual products. In the metaverse, the customers can try on virtual clothes via their avatars [51], or project the virtual furniture into the real house through AR [52]. Then, the customers can proceed to preorder. According to the number of preorders, the sellers inform the manufacturers to produce, and then deliver the products to the customers [53]. Besides, AI technology will empower every aspect of metaverse marketplace, such as product packaging design [54], shop visual effects design, promotional texts writing, products display by AI model [55], product's introduction by AI human [56], and AI customer service [57].

The process is divided into two spaces: Physical Space and Virtual Space. In the Virtual Space, Step 1 is to design the product with AI, resulting in an AI-generated product. Step 2 involves displaying the product with an AI model and scene, which includes display with AI Scene and display with AI Model. Step 3 is the try-on phase, where customers can use an AI Avatar for a virtual try-on. In the Physical Space, the process continues with Step 4, where the customer pre-orders the product from the seller. Step 5 involves the seller informing the manufacturer to produce the physical product. Step 6 is the production of the physical product by the manufacturer. Finally, Step 7 is the delivery of the product to the customer. Customers can enter the metaverse shop with an AI Avatar.

6.1.2 Gaming and social networking

One class of gaming in the metaverse environment is location-based gaming (LBG). LBG is gaining popularity and is believed to be the future of video gaming where a player's everyday experience (e.g., moving around the city) is interleaved with the extraordinary experience of a game. These games deliver an experience that changes according to the player's locations and actions. In LBG, a user equipped with a GPS-enabled handset (e.g., a mobile phone) can play a video game that combines a player's real world (i.e., his physical location) with a virtual world on the handset. The physical location becomes part of the game board, and the player's movement directly influences the gaming progress (and may affect the game character and/or environment). Pokemon GO [58] and Zombies, Run! [59] are examples of LBG.

Another form of metaverse games integrates a physical environment with a corresponding virtual model. Here, RFIDs and sensors are used to capture the information about the players’ current context, which is transmitted to a server. The server (which may be controlled by another player) follows the game rules and relays back to the physical players some information that helps them to proceed (e.g., locations of enemies in the vicinity). Examples of this category of games include Tourality [60] and Wanderer [61]. Social networking can also be conducted in the metaverse. A person in a certain location in the physical space can detect a friend at the same location in the virtual space, and they may fight together against some enemies in the virtual space. Similarly, two “comrades” who fight together in the virtual space can detect each other when they are near to each other in the physical space, giving opportunity for more social interaction. Users may form interest groups to share information and artifacts, and trade user-created contents and virtual valuables, including nonfungible tokens (NFT). They may use the metaverse to conduct consumer-to-consumer or business-to-consumer sales of physical world products.

Story-gameplay is an emerging form of gaming that combines both game and social networking in the metaverse. Based on the story setting, players act as one of the story roles and interact with each other to achieve their goal from the first-person perspective. This form of gaming allows users to experience the story in a highly immersive manner. As an example, in the movie “Ready Player One” [62], the players enter the “Shining Theater” to interact with immersive 3D scene, reveal the truth, and accomplish the mission. Recently, some platforms have started to build story-gameplay metaverses. Let us consider the example in Fig. 3 [63], players select one story from the “Story Hall”, enter the story metaverse, roleplay, interact with the other players or AI NPCs (nonplayer characters), and may also obtain tradable NFT assets. Story-gameplay may also enhance the entertainment experience of other sectors, such as movie and tourism industries. In the movie industry, audiences may shift from watching movies with predetermined endings to engaging in the movies with open endings. Audiences may join the movies by playing certain movie's roles and deciding the plots direction. In the tourism industry, the content of a game may consist of real events that had taken place in the history, which enables tourists to have better understanding about the culture and history in a fun way.

The infographic illustrates the following process: At the top, there is a section labeled Story Hall showing a virtual environment with various story options. Arrows point from the Story Hall to the Story-based metaverses section, depicting different virtual environments. Below, there are three sections: Social networking with friends showing a person sitting on a bench, Interactive scene showing an interactive object, and Tradable asset showing a logo with the text Find Trauman.

It would be interesting to witness the development of a multibillion dollar industry of e-commerce, games, and social networking in tandem with the infrastructure and technology landscape.

In the following part of this chapter, we will focus on AI and blockchain technologies that power the construction of metaverse. Specifically, emphasis on: (1) AI technology that facilitates various content generation and personalized interaction in the metaverse and (2) blockchain technology that offers the economic base to the metaverse. We will discuss how AI and blockchain can effectively support to build the metaverse, and further introduce the data-related challenges that arousing from applying these technologies in the metaverse.

6.2 AI for metaverse

AI technology is the driving force of the metaverse. It is capable of meeting the demands for highly personalized services, providing infinite content resources, and making the effective and strong connections between massive users and contents.

The metaverse needs a large amount of digital contents. However, it is far from enough to meet such huge and diverse content demands only by human works. The multimodal AIGC technology opens the doors to solving this problem [64]. The multimodal AIGC can generate cross-modal contents based on the pretrained models, such as texts, images, music, videos, and 3D models [65]. For example, stable diffusion [66] is able to generate photo-realistic images from texts based on latent diffusion models (LDM); make-a-video [67] is capable of generating videos by inputting texts, images or videos; MusicLM [68] and MusicGen [69] can turn texts into music; and DreamFusion [70] and Magic3D [71] can produce 3D models from texts. By composing these content elements together, novels, movies, games, and other more complicated content forms could be obtained. Taking game design as an example, as shown in Fig. 4, AIGC technology can be applied in each stage of the work process, e.g., the plot generation [72], character and props design, dubbing and sound effects [73], character motion effects, 3D modeling of characters and game scenes [74], and code programming. The multimodal AIGC technology will greatly improve the speed and quality of the creation, and bring infinite contents to the metaverse. It is one of the key factors to promote the metaverse development.

The process starts with the creator inputting text. This text is processed by AI inference models, which include: AI image model for story cover, clue card, texture; AI text model for story content; AI 3D model for 3D model; AI music model for background music; AI panorama model for panorama; AI NPC model for NPC. The elements generated by these models are then dragged to build a 3D scene, resulting in a 3D scene story-gameplay.

To support a large number of users and massive amount of contents in the metaverse, it is critical to establish effective user-to-user or user-to-content connections for the metaverse long-term development. Graph neural network (GNN) exactly addresses this problem. GNNs are the deep learning models capable of working with graph-structured data [75]. It specializes in performing a variety of graph network-related tasks, such as link prediction, node classification, and graph generation, by effectively capturing the features and topology of nodes and edges in the graph. For example, by constructing heterogeneous GNNs, we can mine the potential relationships among various entity types; by constructing dynamic GNNs, we can deal with the problem of time-varying relationships among entities [76]. In the metaverse, supported by GNN technology, users’ social behaviors and patterns can be dynamically analyzed. The potential connections among users and contents can be deeply mined. This can help to make more accurate friend and content recommendations [77]. Therefore, the users can explore and establish closer connections in the metaverse, which will promote the long-term development of the metaverse social network.

From the perspective of data, there are still many challenges for applying the AI technology in the metaverse. The current LLMs expose serious problems of data leakage. Take ChatGPT as an example, OpenAI released a report in March 2023 [78] showing that ChatGPT malfunctioned and caused data leakage due to the bugs in Redis open-source library. This event resulted in some users being able to access other users’ personal information and chat contents. According to a survey from the data security company Cyberhaven [79], a great deal of sensitive information, such as the company's confidential documents or internal customer data, is provided to LLMs through the users’ inquiries and interactions. These sensitive data are sent to the server backend and are further added to the model-training database without any desensitization processing. These data are always at risk of being leaked. The metaverse is a comprehensive place to satisfy the users’ lives, works, and various activities. It involves a large amount of privacy data such as the user's biometric information, digital assets, and business behaviors. It is an urgent issue to effectively protect data privacy and security during the AI training and reasoning process [80]. In addition, there remain many challenges that need to be further addressed, for example, how to solve the issues of data consistency during the data collecting process, how to improve the efficiency for training on massive and dynamic data, and how to deal with the problems of the credibility and bias of AI-generated results.

6.3 Blockchain for metaverse

The attractive features of blockchain, such as decentralization, data immutability, information transparency, and network openness and autonomy [81], make it become the technical cornerstone for building the next generation of value internet. Blockchain is an indispensable technology for the metaverse. It empowers the decentralized identity authentication [29], digital asset verification and circulation [82], and decentralized autonomous organization [33] in the metaverse, which provides a powerful and reliable economic base for the metaverse.

Decentralized identity (DID) is a blockchain-based digital identity system [29]. DID will become the main solution for managing identities in the metaverse. The traditional identity systems are dominated by the centralized authorities. They store the user's identity data and are in charge of the data verification and authorization. As a result, the users fully lose the control of their own identities [83]. And the users’ information is at risk of being tampered or stolen. Also, the identities registered in different organizations are incompatible with each other. In DID solution, the user's personal information and the credential information issued by different organizations are stored on the blockchain or in user's digital wallet in the form of encrypted data [84]. The identity verification does not rely on the issuer of the credential. Instead, the user can decide for themselves to selectively reveal partial identity information to different organizations through personal digital signatures. Furthermore, combined with zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) technology, users can prove their permissions without giving out any identity information [35]. In general, DID can protect the identity privacy and prove its credibility at the same time. It is able to achieve the goal that the identity data are owned by users themselves.

The vision of the metaverse is to build a digital world that is closely connected with the real world and is able to meet all demands of people's works, lives, and economic activities [85]. The resources in the real world can be transformed into digital assets and circulated in the metaverse. Likewise, the digital resources in the metaverse can also locate the equivalent objects or rights in the real world [86]. However, with the traditional Web2 solution, the digital contents are easy to be copied, tampered or stolen, which can’t protect the ownership and scarcity of digital contents. Blockchain technology provides the credible approach to the digital contents authentication and also supports the efficient economic operation in the metaverse. Blockchain technology enables the digital contents to become the easy-to-circulate digital assets [87]. A nonfungible token (NFT) issued on the blockchain is used to prove the authenticity and record the ownership of digital assets. NFT has features like indivisibility, nontampering, and nonreplicability [88]. NFT can be used to mark the ownership of various digital assets, such as digital artworks, video games, music, and digital lands [88]. In the metaverse, the users not only can use tokens to trade the ownership of NFT [89], but also can carry out diverse innovative financial activities based on NFT, such as staking and insurance [90]. With the blockchain, the above-mentioned financial behaviors are easily registered, verified, and traced, which empowers efficient economic operations.

Decentralized autonomous organization (DAO) [33] is an organizational model adapted to the metaverse. Different from traditional hierarchical organizations, DAO is collective decision-making in a distributed, transparent, and trustminimized manner. The consensus mechanism and execution methods of DAO are coded in blockchain-based smart contract, which could be operated autonomously [91]. Benefiting from the features of smart contracts such as constraint-in-advance, immutable, and event-trigger, DAO is empowered to form the organizations in a lower-trust mode [92]. This encourages the users to be willing to engage extensively in global collaboration in the metaverse. DAO incentivizes the members to participate and collaborate through tokens issued on the blockchain. As a type of encrypted digital credential, token contains a variety of attributes, such as the circulating currency, the value-added equity, and the usable real rights [93]. According to the attributes and usage of tokens, DAO adjusts the corresponding issuance volume, lock-up period, and distribution methods to make members profit from their rights. This could facilitate the collaborations among DAO members, optimize DAO resource allocation, and improve DAO governance model [94].

From the perspective of data, there are still many challenges for applying the blockchain technology in the metaverse, for example:

  1. (1) At early stage, each node in the blockchain network is required to back up all the data. Blockchain utilizes data redundancy to ensure data immutability. However, in metaverse scenario, data volume will increase fiercely with the rapid expansion of the applications. The highly redundant massive data will bring serious memory burden to blockchain nodes [95]. When data volume exceeds the storage capacity of most nodes, the difficulty for evil actions will reduce greatly. In this case, the immutability and reliability of blockchain cannot be guaranteed, which will bring fatal security problems. Currently, many studies have proposed new on-chain storage solutions [96], and also on-chain and off-chain collaborative storage solutions [97]. However, there are still a lot of challenges in reducing the node memory burden, strengthening data integrity, and improving data reliability.
  2. (2) In the current industry, there exist various blockchain networks for different application fields and performance requirements. Since the consensus model and hash algorithm of one blockchain may differ from the other, different blockchain networks are hard to exchange information [98]. The information silo is an obstacle for the metaverse development. The data interoperability across different blockchains, which is the ability to share and utilize the data and exchange various digital assets securely among different blockchains, is a significant challenge in the metaverse.

7 Conclusion

The marriage between AI and Web3 marks a pivotal step toward the future of a sustainable digital economy. We explore how AI, with its ability to enhance automation and intelligence, and Web3, with its decentralized, trust-less framework, complement each other to overcome the limitations of current digital systems. AI alone, while powerful, struggles with issues of trust, transparency, and fair incentive distribution. Web3, rooted in blockchain, fills this gap by offering decentralized governance, secure data management, and tokenized incentives. Yet, significant challenges remain in areas like data privacy, transparency, and governance. Web3’s decentralized nature offers solutions to these challenges, promoting secure collaboration, fair data usage, and equitable value sharing. The fusion of AI's automation with Web3’s decentralized systems provides the necessary framework for creating a fair, transparent, and sustainable digital ecosystem.

In conclusion, the convergence of these technologies not only enhances current business models but also paves the way for novel applications that will redefine the global digital landscape. The future of the digital economy lies in this harmonious integration, where intelligence and decentralization coalesce to drive innovation, trust, and long-term growth.
