Chapter 18 The third wave of technological advancements in blockchain: Exploring the application of zero-knowledge proofs technology

  1. Jincheng Zhenga
  2. Swee-Won Loa
  3. Tao Panb
  4. Anna Kaplanc
  5. a School of Business, Singapore University of Social Sciences, Singapore, Singapore
  6. b Beosin, Singapore, Singapore
  7. c Least Authority, Berlin, Germany

Abstract

This chapter provides an overview of zero-knowledge proof (ZKP), a cryptographic technique enabling private verification of information between parties while preserving data privacy and self-sovereignty. It covers the primary applications of ZKP, compares the latest advances in various ZKP technologies, and discusses their innovative combinations with blockchain systems. Possible future trends in this field are also explored.

Keywords

Zero-knowledge proof

Privacy

zk-SNARK

zk-STARK

1 Introduction

If we consider Bitcoin the first innovation that revolutionizes the meaning of a payment system and Ethereum the second significant advancement in reducing the cost of trust using smart contracts, then zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) represents the third pivotal advancement in blockchain technology.

Zero-knowledge proofs (or ZKPs) convey no additional knowledge other than the correctness of the proposition in question [1]. They offer a nearly risk-free method for sharing a user's data with third parties for various purposes while maintaining data sovereignty and privacy. Users can prove the authenticity or validity of their sensitive data while having complete control over the storage of their data. A primary example will be the authentication mechanism—traditionally, users must set up a username and password with a third-party application and supply this information for verification before being granted access to the application. This setting means that the third-party application gains knowledge about the users’ passwords, which creates risks for impersonation or user preference analysis. As detailed in the subsequent sections, ZKP allows users to prove their eligibility to access an application without revealing their identity other than the fact that he/she is eligible. Such data sovereignty is significant in decentralized systems (such as the blockchain) and in easing compliance with data privacy regulations.

In other words, ZKP's application in blockchain enables users to perform transactions securely and privately on public decentralized networks. Apart from privacy, ZKP is also used to improve the scalability of these networks.

This chapter aims to serve as a definitive reference on the evolution of ZKP, its variants, and their applications in Web3. Section 2 presents an overview of ZKP, including its properties and the concepts of interactive and non-interactive ZKPs, respectively. Section 3 discusses ZKP's Web3 applications, including the provision of privacy protection in a decentralized peer-to-peer payment system and serving as one of the Layer-2 blockchain scalability solutions. Subsequently, Section 4 details the main variants of ZKP, including the Zero-Knowledge Succinct Non-Interactive Argument of Knowledge (zk-SNARK), Zero-Knowledge Scalable Transparent Knowledge Argument (zk-STARK), and recursive zk-SNARK, as well as some projects that deploys these variants. A forecast of the future trends and potential advancements in ZKP's application are discussed in Section 5.

2 Zero-knowledge proofs

In the work of Goldwasser et al. [1], the zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) protocol is a zero-knowledge interactive proof system, where the Prover and the Verifier must interact with each other before the Verifier can conclude with a high probability that the Prover knows the secret. A subsequent work by Blum et al. [2] proposed a non-interactive variant of zero-knowledge proofs that achieves the same outcome without needing interactions between the Prover and the Verifier as long as both parties share a common reference string. The work by Blum et al. [2] laid the foundation for the subsequent development of non-interactive ZKPs widely used in blockchain applications.

In this section, we will examine the properties of ZKP protocols and the concepts of interactive and non-interactive ZKP, respectively.

2.1 Properties

A ZKP protocol must satisfy the properties of completeness, soundness, and zero-knowledge(ness). Referencing Blum et al. [2]:

  • • Completeness: The probability of (a Prover) succeeding in proving a true theorem is overwhelming.
  • • Soundness: The probability of (a Prover) succeeding in proving a false theorem is negligible.
  • • Zero-knowledge: The proof gives no information but the validity of the theorem.

A ZKP has a small (and negligible) probability of producing a rationality error, meaning a cheating Prover can deceive the Verifier into believing that a false statement is true.

To this end, we expand the discussion on the properties of ZKP. The completeness property states that if the Prover is honest (i.e., it indeed knows the “secret”), then the Prover will eventually (for interactive ZKPs) convince the Verifier that it knows the secret. The soundness property states that the Prover can only convince the Verifier if it knows the secret and that the verification procedure cannot be “tricked” into accepting a false statement. The zero-knowledge property requires that a ZKP protocol does not reveal any information to the Verifier apart from the fact that the Prover knows the secret.

The Alibaba Cave story illustrated in Quisquater et al. [3] shows an instance of the zero-knowledge(ness) property. In the story, the fact that Mick Ali proved that he knew the secret to opening the cave door, yet the judges and experts were unable to tell the difference between the real tape (taken by a reporter on Mick Ali's actual proving process) and the simulated tape (taken and edited by a jealous reporter on a stage actor who looked like Mick Ali and does not know the secret) showed that no information was revealed to the reporter or any third-party observers apart from the fact that Mick Ali knows the secret. In other words, a true zero-knowledge protocol guarantees that information exchanged during the proving process is indistinguishable from information generated by a pseudorandom simulator.

2.2 Working mechanism

In this section, we examine in more detail the two main types of ZKP, namely interactive and non-interactive ZKP. The protocols involve two parties: the Prover and the Verifier.

2.2.1 Interactive zero-knowledge proof

An interactive ZKP protocol consists of three steps between the Prover and the Verifier: Commit, Challenge, and Response. To prove that the Prover knows the solution to a hard problem (i.e., the secret), both the Prover and Verifier start with sharing a common input, that is, the hard problem/statement to be proven.

  • • Commit: The Prover uses its secret information and a pseudorandom number to transform the hard problem into another hard problem that is isomorphic to the original problem. The Prover then commits to the solution of the new problem using a bit-commitment scheme and sends the Commitment (Commitment schemes are cryptographic protocols that enable a party to compute a commitment to a value v while keeping v secret. The commitment can later be “opened” to show the value v that has been committed to during the committing phase.) to the Verifier.
  • • Challenge: The Verifier then flips a coin that gives either a 0 or a 1 and sends the result as the Challenge to the Prover.
  • • Response: Based on the Verifier's Challenge, the Prover sends a Response that is either proof that the original and new problems are isomorphic (i.e., two different solutions to two related problems) or opens the solution to the Commitment.

In an interactive ZKP, these steps are repeated sufficiently many times until the Verifier is convinced that the Prover knows the secret information. The protocol's proof transcript will consist of ({Commitment1, Challenge1, Response1}, …, {Commitmentn, Challengen, Responsen}) for round 1 to round n. Since a commitment scheme is binding (Binding means that after the commitment for the value v has been computed and given to the other party, the committing party cannot change the value v anymore.), if the Prover does not know the secret, it has only a 50% chance of correctly guessing the Verifier's Challengei in each round i and preparing for the corresponding Responsei. The Prover can only consistently return the correct Responsei if the Prover knows the secret information. Hence, the proving process can be repeated multiple times until the Verifier is satisfied that the probability of the Prover returning the correct response without knowledge of the secret information becomes sufficiently low or negligible. If the probability of the Prover guessing the correct answer without knowledge of the secret, s, in each round is 1/2 and the interaction is repeated 10 times, the probability of the Prover guessing the Challenge correctly in every round is only 0.097%. Therefore, it is highly unlikely that the Verifier will be convinced if the Prover does not know the secret, s.

2.2.2 Non-interactive zero-knowledge proof

A non-interactive ZKP protocol, as its name suggests, does not require back-and-forth communication between the Prover and the Verifier. The challenge and response process, which forms the interactive part of a ZKP protocol, is replaced by a common reference string (CRS) shared between the Prover and Verifier [2] following a general method called the Fiat-Shamir heuristic [4]. Essentially, the “challenge” is constructed using a suitable hash function H to construct a “digital signature” of a message that comprises the Commitment.

A non-interactive ZKP basic protocol works as follows to prove that the Prover knows the solution to a difficult problem [5]:

  • • The Prover uses the secret information s and n random numbers to transform the hard problem into a set of n different hard problems that are isomorphic to the original problem. The Prover then creates one Commitment to the solution of each of the n hard problems.
  • • The Prover uses all of the n Commitments as inputs to a one-way hash function. The first n bits of the hash value will be saved. For each bit i = 0, …, n, the Prover will either prove that the old and ith new hard problems are isomorphic (if bit i is a 0) or open the solution of Commitment i and prove that it is a solution to the ith new hard problem (if bit i is a 1).
  • • The Prover publishes all n Commitments and their proofs/solutions based on the first n bits of the hash value in the previous step.
  • • The Verifier verifies that all the above steps are executed correctly by the Prover.

The above protocol works because the one-way hash function acts as an unbiased random bit generator. The Prover can only successfully cheat if the Prover can predict the first n bits of the hash value. However, the hash value is calculated based on the n Commitments as inputs to the one-way hash function; the Prover cannot predict the output of the hash function because it cannot predict its inputs—the Commitments are only known after the Prover solves the new hard problems.

Non-interactive ZKP is a breakthrough in ZKP technology as it promotes the development of using zero-knowledge-proof systems today. The two main non-interactive ZKP protocols that are popularly used are the Zero-Knowledge Succinct Non-Interactive Argument of Knowledge (zk-SNARK) and the Zero-Knowledge Scalable Transparent Argument of Knowledge (zk-STARK). We will review both in Section 4.

3 Web3 application of zero-knowledge proof

In the Web3 space, zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) protocols are primarily used to provide privacy protection on public blockchain transactions and smart contracts that enable decentralized applications. Another application for ZKP is to improve blockchain scalability in terms of either reducing blockchain storage size or increasing transaction throughput (transactions per second, TPS).

3.1 Privacy protection

In decentralized public blockchains such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, transactions and smart contracts must be transparent for miners or validators to verify transaction validity and maintain a publicly verifiable distributed ledger. The transparency limits the applicability of public blockchain for commercial and business use cases, where data privacy is crucial. Furthermore, in decentralized public networks, users have inherent distrust among each other, and bandwidth and storage resources are scarce. Hence, interactive proof protocols are barely an option. These results in non-interactive ZKPs becoming a natural solution to address the privacy needs in Web3 applications.

3.1.1 Privacy coins and decentralization applications (dApps)

The first and most well-known ZKP application in the Web3 space. It is used to protect user and transaction privacy in the Zcash (ZEC) blockchain [6]. Zcash was created as a fork of the Bitcoin blockchain, but in contrast to Bitcoin, it provides the options for transparent transactions that are similar to Bitcoin and shielded transactions that are protected by ZKP. Zcash achieves this using the Zero-Knowledge Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments of Knowledge (zk-SNARK) protocol, which will be covered in more detail in Section 4.

Another privacy coin that leverages ZKP is Monero (XMR) [7]. Monero was launched in 2014, and all transactions are private by default [8]. Besides ring signatures to conceal the sender's address and stealth addresses to hide the receiver's address, ZKP is used in Monero to hide while allowing proving of the validity of the transaction amounts. Monero uses Ring Confidential Transaction (or RingCT), which employs Pedersen Commitments to ensure that the total input of a transaction equals the total output without revealing the exact amount [9]. In addition, Bulletproofs are used to prove that transaction amounts are positive (to prevent the creation of negative transaction amounts) without revealing the actual transaction amounts [10]. Bulletproofs and Bulletproofs+ [11] are non-interactive ZKPs based on inner-product arguments. They use the Fiat-Shamir heuristic to eliminate the need for interaction. Apart from making transactions private by default, Monero does not require a trusted setup, as its security relies on standard cryptographic assumptions (the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem), while Zcash's zk-SNARKs rely on pairings and polynomial computations.

The zk-SNARK and Zero-Knowledge Scalable Transparent Arguments of Knowledge (zk-STARK) protocols can also enable the private execution of smart contracts on the blockchain. For instance, the Minimum Anti-Collusion Infrastructure (MACI) creates an on-chain decentralized voting system resistant to collusion and coercion by providing voter privacy and allowing public verification of voting results [12]. Specifically, voters should not be able to collude and coordinate votes to influence the outcome of a voting process. They should not fear coercion by external parties and manipulate their votes for rewards or fear of being identified/punished. In MACI, zk-SNARKs were used to allow participants to prove the correctness and validity of their votes without revealing what they voted for. In addition, public key infrastructure is also used, where users use their public key to encrypt their votes. At the end of the voting period, the coordinator uses ZKP to prove that all messages have been processed correctly. This is done without revealing the contents of the messages or the voters’ identities.

3.1.2 Mixers

Mixers are used in cryptocurrency ecosystems to enhance user privacy by obfuscating the linkage between a transaction's sending and receiving ends. A straightforward example of a mixer is Bitcoin's CoinJoin algorithm [13], where two or more users agree to pool their funds as inputs to a Bitcoin transaction and redistribute them to separate output addresses that appear unlinked to the CoinJoin users. In this case, users gain plausible deniability, as any observing third parties cannot link the input and output to a specific individual. However, CoinJoin keeps information about the sender, receiver, and transaction amounts in the clear.

Zero-knowledge mixers use ZKP to achieve the same objective of delinking the sender and receiver addresses. Specifically, zero-knowledge mixers are smart contracts that use zk-SNARKs for users to prove that they contributed funds to the mixer pool (of inputs) without disclosing any transaction details. Upon verification, the mixer issues a “receipt” to the depositing user. During withdrawal, users use ZKP to prove that they have the right receipt to withdraw a certain amount.

Tornado Cash is a popular non-custodial zk-SNARK-based mixer that enhances users’ anonymity by hiding their identity and linkage to the funds [14]. It appears as a smart contract on the Ethereum blockchain, and it allows users to deposit funds (ether or any ERC20 tokens) into the smart contract. The smart contract generates a zk-SNARK proof, which the user can subsequently use to prove his/her ownership of the fund.

Compared to CoinJoin, the first instance of the “mixer” concept, ZKP-based mixers maximize user privacy protection as they do not gain any information about a transaction or a user from deposit to withdrawal from the mixer pool.

3.2 Blockchain scalability

Traditional blockchains like Bitcoin and Ethereum rely on decentralized networks of nodes to validate and record transactions. This approach requires each node to process and store every transaction. As the number of blockchain users increases, the volume of on-chain transactions increases, which results in congestion. Various scaling solutions have been proposed to address this issue, and they can generally be classified as Layer 1 and Layer 2 solutions. Layer 1 solutions involve changes made directly to the blockchain protocol, and examples include sharding, block size adjustments, and modification of transaction format (such as the use of a more compact Schnorr signature in Bitcoin).

On the other hand, Layer 2 solutions operate on top of the existing blockchain (e.g., Bitcoin and Ethereum) and do not make any modifications directly to the main chain. The general concept is to process transactions off the main chain and only update the main chain with the processing outcome. Examples of Layer 2 solutions are state channels (e.g., the Lightning Network and the Raiden Network), sidechains (e.g., Polygon), and rollups. Among them, rollups process transactions off-chain and bundle them into a single transaction settled on the main chain. The two types of rollups are Optimistic Rollup and zero-knowledge rollup (ZK-Rollup). Optimistic Rollup assumes transactions are valid by default and submit the batch of transactions to the main chain with a challenge period; transactions are only reversed in the event of a fraudulent transaction being detected and substantiated by a fraud proof before the challenge period expires. As a result, users must endure a seven-day waiting period to retrieve their funds following a withdrawal request.

Optimistic Rollup has been strategically designed to seamlessly integrate with the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM), ensuring smooth integration with existing Ethereum tools and smart contracts. This compatibility factor has significantly contributed to the rapid development and widespread adoption of Optimistic Rollup solutions, such as Arbitrum [15] and Optimism (https://www.optimism.io/).

ZK-Rollup, as its name suggests, uses a zero-knowledge proof (ZKP)-based approach. The ZK-Rollup protocol aggregates multiple transactions into a single batch off-chain, with succinct proof of validity submitted to the main chain [16]. This allows for significant scalability and efficiency improvements while maintaining the underlying blockchain's security guarantees. The main chain simply verifies and stores the proof and updates the state without processing and storing the details of every transaction. Using ZK-Rollups, developers can design lightweight decentralized applications (dApps) that can run on common hardware, such as mobile phones, which is more conducive to the popularization of Web3.

Table 1 highlights the differences between Optimistic Rollup and ZK-Rollup. Overall, Optimistic Rollup has a more mature ecosystem and is relatively straightforward in its implementation. Its reliance on economic incentives and game theory for security and transaction validation will require more user involvement to detect fraud than ZK-Rollup. Although Optimistic Rollup has lower storage efficiency, it conversely provides a higher degree of decentralization due to data availability. Its compatibility with the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) makes it easier to deploy in existing Ethereum-based dApps, hence resulting in a more mature ecosystem compared to ZK-Rollup. ZK-Rollup, despite its complexity, benefits from a more scalable, efficient, and secure solution.

Table 1

A comparison between Optimistic Rollup and ZK-Rollup.
Optimistic Rollups ZK-Rollups
Security model Economic incentives and game theory Cryptographic proofs
Transaction validation Fraud proof submission within the challenge period Invalid transactions will not be packaged into proof and submitted to the chain
Finality Several hours to 1 week Immediate, as soon as the proof is verified
Storage efficiency All the transaction data with data compression techniques Only the succinct proof generated by zk-SNARK or zk-STARK
Ethereum virtual machine (EVM) compatibility Compatible Incompatible
Implementation complexity The development difficulty is relatively lower The development difficulty is relatively higher due to the use of complex cryptographic components
Ecosystem maturity More matured Some launched the main network, and more are in the test network stage, which is still in the early development phase

It is also worth noting that the EVM was originally designed without including zero-knowledge proofing technology. Vitalik Buterin, the founder of Ethereum, notes that while the ZK-Rollup presents technical complexities in the short term, it will outperform the Optimistic Rollup in the ongoing scalability race [17]. Hence, choosing between Optimistic Rollup and ZK-Rollup will depend highly on the project's available resources and long-term scalability needs.

4 The main variants of zero-knowledge proof

The main variants of zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) protocols used in the Web3 space are the Zero-Knowledge Succinct Non-Interactive Argument of Knowledge (zk-SNARK), Zero-Knowledge Scalable Transparent Knowledge Argument (zk-STARK), and recursive zk-SNARK [18]. This section presents an overview of each variant and reviews some projects deploying these privacy-protection protocols.

4.1 zk-SNARK

zk-SNARK is best known for enabling private transactions in the Zcash blockchain. Table 2 defines zk-SNARK, and this section presents an overview of zk-SNARK and some of its applications.

Table 2

The definition of zk-SNARK.
zk (Zero-Knowledge) The Prover proves to the Verifier that a statement is true without revealing any information beyond the validity of the statement itself
S (Succinct) The proofs can be verified quickly (i.e., within a few milliseconds) with a small proof size (i.e., within a few hundred bytes)
N (Non-Interactive) There is only one message sent from the Prover to the Verifier
ARK (ARgument of Knowledge) Proof of computational rationality: It is difficult for a Prover without knowledge of the secret to calculate an effective zero-knowledge proof; for the Verifier using polynomial time, rationality is established

4.1.1 Overview of zk-SNARK

For zk-SNARK's usage in Zcash, specific transaction arithmetic circuits are created (e.g., a circuit to verify that hash calculation is conducted correctly). In the proving process, the Prover encodes the input (e.g., input to the hash function), output (e.g., the hash value), and intermediate states of the circuit as polynomials. The Prover then creates commitments to these polynomials, ensuring that the actual data is hidden while allowing verification. If these polynomials satisfy the “QAP equation” for a target polynomial (representing the structure of the circuit), then one can conclude that the computation is correct. The Fiat-Shamir heuristic is used in this process, where the Prover hashes the commitment to the polynomials and uses the resulting hash value as the “challenge.” The Prover then computes a response to the challenge. Using zk-SNARKs, Zcash allows users to hide information about a transaction's sender, receiver, and/or transaction amount while allowing miners on the Zcash public network to verify the correct ownership and validity of the transaction.

On the scalability end, most ZK-Rollups that use zk-SNARK follow the following steps:

  1. 1. Layer 2 users create transactions and submit them to the rollup operator for processing.
  2. 2. Transactions are then aggregated, and a succinct proof is created for the aggregated set of transactions. The proof allows Verifiers to verify that the set of transactions is valid without revealing any transaction data.
  3. 3. The proof is sent to the main chain (Layer 1), where a smart contract verifies it. Upon successful verification, the proof is added to the main chain and its state is updated.

It is important to note that zk-SNARK requires trust. The common reference string (CRS) generated by multiple parties through a trusted setup ceremony serves as a public parameter in Zcash to supply pseudorandomness to the target polynomials. In other words, the CRS contains parameters necessary for constructing and verifying proofs, and hence, the randomness used in the generation of the CRS must be destroyed upon completion of the setup ceremony; exposure could enable the creation of valid fake proofs. To ensure the security of the trusted setup, it is important for users to trust that participants in the trusted setup ceremony are honest. However, evaluating the honesty of participants is not always possible. Table 3 shows the strengths and weaknesses of zk-SNARK.

Table 3

Strengths and weaknesses of zk-SNARK.
Strength Weakness
Higher throughput:
Verification of zk-SNARK proofs is fast, at a few milliseconds. This allows more efficient transaction validations		 Trust setting:
zk-SNARK requires a trusted setup ceremony to create the Common Reference String (CRS) for creating and validating proofs. If the ceremony participants cheat, zk-SNARK proofs can be faked
Smaller proof size:
Proofs generated by zk-SNARK proofs are succinct, at a few hundred bytes, even when the statements to be proven are very large		 Threat from quantum computing:
zk-SNARK uses Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), which is currently considered robust in terms of security. However, ongoing advancements in quantum computing pose a potential threat to its security model
Operational complexity:
The CRS is specific to the presetup arithmetic circuits; if there is an update or upgrade of the circuits, a new CRS will need to be generated with another round of the trusted setup ceremony

4.1.2 Projects using zk-SNARK

In this section, we list several projects that use zk-SNARKs to achieve privacy protection. This is not an exhaustive list, and the descriptions are in no particular order.

4.1.2.1 Polygon Hermez

In 2021, Polygon acquired Hermez for $250 million, marking the first comprehensive merger between two blockchain networks. Polygon utilizes Hermez's ZKP technology and tools to advance the development of zkEVM.

Hermez 1.0 was initially designed as a payment platform that orchestrates a sequence of off-chain transactions, allowing users to transfer ERC-20 tokens between Hermez accounts seamlessly. This version achieves an impressive throughput, with transactions per second reaching up to 2000.

The transition to Hermez 2.0 represents a significant advancement, as it transparently executes Ethereum transactions, including smart contracts with zero-knowledge verification. Hermez 2.0 maintains full compatibility with Ethereum, requiring minimal modifications to smart contract code. This feature is useful for developers who want to deploy Layer 1 projects on Polygon Hermez.

Hermez 1.0 relies on zk-SNARK proofs, while Hermez 2.0 uses both zk-SNARK and zk-STARK proofs simultaneously. In the context of 2.0, zk-STARK proofs are used to verify the effectiveness of off-chain transactions. However, verifying zk-STARK proofs on the main chain can be costly. To address this issue, zk-SNARK proofs can be introduced to efficiently verify zk-STARK, reducing the computational burden on the main chain.

4.1.2.2 ZkSync

Matter Labs launched ZkSync 1.0 [19] in 2020, primarily focusing on transactions. ZkSync 2.0 was publicly launched on the main network in March 2023, introducing significant evolution by supporting smart contracts.

ZkSync employs a unique approach to handling smart contracts. Solidity source code for smart contracts in Ethereum is compiled into Yul, an intermediate language compatible with different EVMs. Yul code is then recompiled into a custom, circuit-compatible bytecode set designed for zkEVM within ZkSync using the LLVM compiler framework. This innovative method simplifies the decentralization of the proof process while maintaining robust performance by eliminating the need to prove all EVM execution steps through higher-level code.

The architecture of zkEVM in ZkSync exhibits flexibility and the potential to expand language support. New compiler front ends can seamlessly integrate support for Rust, Javascript, or other languages. This strategic enhancement increases the versatility of the zkEVM architecture, fostering a more inclusive environment for developers.

4.1.2.3 Aztec

Aztec is the first hybrid ZK-Rollup that can implement public and private smart contracts in one environment. This is a zero-knowledge execution environment, not zkEVM. Confidentiality and audibility are achieved by merging public and private execution into a single mixed rollup, such as the private transaction of a public automated market maker, the private messaging of a public game, the private voting of a public DAO, and so on.

4.2 zk-STARK

zk-STARK is an acronym for Zero-Knowledge Scalable Transparent Knowledge Argument. It is a transparent ZKP system that scales exponentially faster than database size, enabling scalable, transparent, and postquantum secure computational integrity in sensitive data [20]. Table 4 shows the definition of zk-STARK.

Table 4

The definition of zk-STARK.
zk (Zero-Knowledge) The Prover proves to the Verifier that a statement is true without revealing any information beyond the validity of the statement itself
S (Scalable) Ability to perform batch verification of proofs and the verification time increases logarithmically with the number of proofs
T (Transparent) Using publicly available randomness to generate parameters, anyone can verify the correctness of a proof without reliance on a trusted setup
ARK (ARgument of Knowledge) Proof of computational rationality: It is difficult for a Prover without knowledge of the secret to calculate an effective zero-knowledge proof; for the Verifier using polynomial time, rationality is established

4.2.1 Overview of zk-STARK

zk-STARK uses arithmetization to encode the computations (to be proven correct) into a series of polynomials over a finite field using Algebraic Intermediate Representation (AIR). For a computation, the polynomials are constraints defining the rules that a correct computation step must satisfy. The Prover then commits to a polynomial or a set of data points by hashing them into a Merkle tree. The Merkle tree's leaf nodes correspond to values derived from the polynomial commitments, and the Merkle root compactly represents these commitments. The proof generated by the Prover will then be the specific Merkle path of a commitment that allows the Verifier to reconstruct the root hash. The Verifier reconstructs the Merkle tree using the provided hashes and verifies that the data corresponds to the commitment.

In addition to the above, the Prover will prove that this set of polynomials indeed consists of low-degree polynomials. The proving method uses the Fast Reed-Solomon Interactive Oracle Proofs of Proximity (the FRI protocol). The FRI protocol proves the proximity of a function to a low-degree polynomial. Low-degree polynomials of degree d can be uniquely determined by evaluating them at d + 1 points. Their use is crucial in zk-STARK because the probability of an incorrect low-degree polynomial passing as a valid proof is exceedingly low compared to high-degree polynomials that could hide inconsistencies or errors when the number of evaluating points is high. Using Reed-Solomon as a way of error correction also allows for detecting and correcting errors in the encoded polynomials.

In a normal interactive proof, the Verifier will send a small number of data points for the Prover to return with the result of the computation based on these data points. zk-STARK similarly uses the Fiat-Shamir heuristic, where random challenges are replaced with hash values. The zero-knowledgeness is ensured by using a secure hash function.

Due to zk-STARK's design, it can handle larger input sizes without an exponential increase in the verification time, and this corresponds to its scalability characteristic. In addition, zk-STARK does not require a trusted ceremony to set up a common reference string because of its use of polynomials and Merkle trees, which contributes to its transparent characteristic. Due to its scalable and transparent properties, zk-STARK can be used in various applications besides ZK-Rollup. A detailed overview of zk-STARK and its processes can be found in Ref. [21]. Table 5 shows the strengths and weaknesses of zk-STARK.

Table 5

Strengths and weaknesses of zk-STARK.
Strengths Weaknesses
Greater scalability:
Practical proof sizes, proof generation, and verification times even when dealing with large input dataset sizes		 Larger proof size:
The proof size increases with a larger input dataset size
Trustless:
zk-STARK relies on the security of the hash function and thus does not require any trusted setup phase		 Low adoption rate:
zk-SNARK is the first practical application of zero-knowledge proof in blockchain, so most ZK-Rollups adopt zk-SNARK, which has more mature developer systems and tools. Although the Ethereum Foundation also supports zk-STARK, the adoption rate is relatively low, and the basic developer tools need to be improved
Quantum-resistance:
zk-STARK uses a collision-resistant hash function, which is currently considered secure against quantum computers

4.2.2 Projects using zk-STARK

The following subsections list several projects that deploy zk-STARKs. This is not an exhaustive list, and the descriptions are in no particular order.

4.2.2.1 Polygon Miden

Polygon Miden, a scalable Ethereum Layer 2 solution, strategically leverages zk-STARK technology to merge a significant volume of Layer 2 transactions into a single Ethereum transaction. This innovative approach increases processing capacity while reducing transaction costs. In particular, Polygon Miden achieves impressive results even without sharding, with a block generation time of 5 s and a TPS (transactions per second) of over 1000. After integrating sharding, the TPS can reach an impressive 10,000 TPS.

Users can complete withdrawals from Polygon Miden to Ethereum in only 15 min. At the heart of Polygon Miden is its core functionality—a Turing-complete virtual machine (VM) based on zk-STARK, namely the MidenVM. This design choice not only significantly increases the efficiency of contract execution but also streamlines the formal verification process for contracts, making it significantly more accessible and user-friendly.

4.2.2.2 StarkEx and StarkNet

StarkEx stands out as a tailored framework for scaling solutions designed for specific applications. StarkEx leverages low-cost and off-chain computation to generate STARK proofs, which provide evidence of the correct execution of operations. Remarkably, each proof covers a substantial range, from 12,000 to 500,000 transactions. Once the proof is generated, it is transmitted to the STARK verifier in the chain, and the status update is accepted upon successful verification. Notable applications deployed on StarkEx include dYdX (perpetual futures), Immutable X (L2 NFT market), Sorare (digital sports card trading market), and Rhino.fi (cross-chain bridge).

In contrast, StarkNet operates as a permissionless L2 platform, allowing anyone to deploy smart contracts developed in the Cairo language. Contracts deployed on StarkNet can interact with each other, paving the way for the creation of new composable protocols. Unlike StarkEx, where applications are responsible for submitting transactions, StarkNet uses a sequencer to batch transactions and facilitate their processing and certification. StarkNet is particularly well-suited for protocols that require synchronous interaction with others or that extend beyond the application scope of StarkEx. The evolution of StarkNet provides the ability to transplant applications from StarkEx to StarkNet, allowing them to benefit from enhanced composability. Table 6 compares the main differences between zk-SNARK and zk-STARK.

Table 6

Comparison between zk-SNARK and zk-STARK.
zk-SNARK zk-STARK
Proving method Elliptic Curve Cryptography and Quadratic Arithmetic Programs Low-degree polynomials and hash function
Trust model A trusted setup phase is required No trusted setup phase is required
Quantum-resistance The use of public key cryptography is not quantum-resistant The use of a hash function is more quantum-resistant, ensuring longer-term security
Proving
Proof size Constant as input dataset size increases Increases logarithmically as input dataset size increases
Proof generation Proof generation time increases significantly as input dataset size increases Proof generation time increases linearly as input dataset size increases; computation can use parallelization
Verification
Verification time Constant as input dataset size increases Increases logarithmically as input dataset size increases but is still considered practical
Others
Development tools Relatively mature due to its longer development history since Zcash Relatively immature as it is mainly used in the more recently developed ZK-Rollups
Cost efficiency More cost-efficient for on-chain verification Less efficient for on-chain verification due to larger proof sizes

4.3 Comparison between zk-SNARK and zk-STARK

As zk-SNARKs use bilinear pairing and polynomial computations related to specific transaction arithmetic circuits, a trusted setup phase is required to generate a common reference string (CRS) for secure proof generation and verification. If the randomness used during the setup phase is leaked, it will lead to the generation of false proofs. On the other hand, zk-STARK utilizes low-degree polynomials and Merkle trees; its security relies on the security of hash functions and does not require any setup phase.

On the Prover's end, as the size of the input dataset increases, zk-SNARK creates a constant proof size, although the proof computation will increase in complexity, while zk-STARK creates a larger proof size and a linear increase in proof computation. On the Verifier's end, zk-SNARK's verification time is constant while zk-STARK's verification time grows logarithmically with the input dataset size. However, such verification is considered practical because of the more efficient cryptographic and computation algorithms used in zk-STARK.

Hence, the scalability of zk-STARK makes it highly applicable for applications that handle large input datasets or require complex computations. Apart from its application in ZK-Rollups, zk-STARK is also well-suited for proving that smart contract computation steps are correct without revealing the smart contract content. Considering the role of smart contracts in decentralized applications such as Decentralized Finance (DeFi) and Decentralisted Autonomous Organization (DAO), the integration of smart contracts with zk-STARK could significantly advance the development of privacy protection in decentralization applications. However, the fact that zk-STARK generates larger proof sizes with larger input datasets means that its on-chain storage cost is high. This drawback could be circumvented by integrating Layer 2 scalability solutions such as ZK-Rollups.

Table 6 compares the main differences between zk-SNARK and zk-STARK.

4.4 Recursive zk-SNARK

Ordinary ZK-Rollups can only handle one transaction block, which limits the number of transactions they can handle. Recursive zk-SNARK can verify more than one transaction block, merge the SNARKs generated by different Layer 2 blocks into a single proof of validity, and submit it to the Layer 1 chain. Once the Layer 1 chain contract accepts the submitted proof, all of those transactions become valid, greatly increasing the number of transactions that can ultimately be processed per second.

Plonky2 is a new proof mechanism from Polygon Zero that uses recursive zk-SNARK to increase the number of transactions. Recursive SNARK extends the proof generation process by aggregating multiple proofs into a single recursive proof. Plonky2 uses the same technology to reduce the time it takes to generate new block proofs. Plonky2 generates thousands of transactions in parallel and recursively aggregates them into a block proof, so the generation speed is fast. However, the usual proofing mechanism tries to generate the entire block proof at once, which is less efficient. In addition, Plonky2 can generate proofs on consumer devices, solving the hardware centralization problem often associated with SNARK proofs.

5 The future of zero-knowledge proofs technology application

The field of zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) is unique: much effort has been devoted to advancing research in this area in recent years, but many results are relatively new. As a result, the research and development community has yet to answer many interesting questions. At the same time, ZKPs are being implemented in various projects, revealing challenges and fine-tuning the requirements of zero-knowledge technology.

One area of ZKP technology to watch is the discussion of postquantum security of ZKP technology. Publicly verifiable zk-SNARKs are a key component within the field of zero-knowledge technology. However, most widely used publicly verifiable zk-SNARK schemes are not considered quantum-safe. Examples include Groth16, Sonic, Marlin, SuperSonic, and Spartan. These schemes rely on mathematical problems that can be efficiently solved using quantum computers, compromising their security in a postquantum world.

The research community is working hard to find quantum-safe ZKPs that can be used for various statements without any preprocessing phase. Recent examples of state-of-the-art quantum-safe ZKPs include Ligero, Aurora, Fractal, Lattice Bulletproofs, and LPK22. Ligero, Aurora, and Fractal are based on hash functions, while Lattice Bulletproofs and LKP22 are based on lattice functions. Both of these functions are considered to have the potential to be quantum-safe. There is a trend toward generalizing these schemes and increasing their efficiency.

Another aspect to see in the future of zero-knowledge technology is its resilience to attack and the maturity of implementations. As the amount of code written increases, there will be more secure and vetted libraries used for all types of zero-knowledge proofing technology, best practices will be discussed and agreed upon, and common bugs will be identified and communicated. In addition, as the field matures and becomes widely adopted, there will be efforts to standardize protocols and ensure interoperability between different implementations (e.g., the ZKProof project).

Another trend that will continue within the zero-knowledge community is more work on efficient algorithms and possibly specialized hardware. In recent years, significant progress has been made in reducing proof sizes and increasing efficiency for both provers and verifiers. Advances in algorithms, specialized hardware, and computational optimizations can lead to faster and more scalable implementations. The future utility of ZKP technology is expected to benefit from the improved efficiency of existing algorithms. Furthermore, an expansion of the functionality of ZKPs is anticipated. Numerous instances of preprocessing zk-SNARK implementations have been identified in the past. Also, some ZKP technology is used more for its conciseness property than for its zero-knowledge capability.

Finally, another trend we observe in ZKP technology is the intersection of machine learning. The idea is to train large language models in a multiparty setting and use ZKP to verify the computation. This could be useful for the efficiency of current artificial intelligence algorithms, and potential projects emerging in this area seem likely.
